A high-precision mass measurement experiment was then conducted at the CSRe cyclotron facility, where researchers successfully measured the masses of $^{46}$Cl and $^{47}$Cl with high precision, specifically 1100 times and 450 times tighter than previous values, respectively. This breakthrough technique, known as Bρ-defined isochronous mass spectrometry (Bρ-IMS), enables the accurate measurement of rare atomic isotopes' masses with exceptional precision.

The All Quantum Flows initiative aims to create a comprehensive, publicly accessible library of quantum field theory simulations, allowing multiple teams to work together on lattice field theory by providing standardized code and research opportunities. This paper serves as an introduction to this initiative and outlines our methodology for developing standardized code modules, which are then implemented in practice using the example of an Ising model simulation.

Structured text, found in forms like addresses, names, and dates, is becoming increasingly prevalent in image recognition tasks. The current methods for recognizing structured text are largely based on sequence-to-sequence models, but they tend to be prone to errors due to their lack of pre-defined guidelines. In many instances, the correct approach to interpreting certain text elements can be clearly outlined as a regular expression. Our research proposes an efficient technique to incorporate regular expressions into existing structured text recognition frameworks, allowing for more accurate predictions based on predefined patterns. We have tested this method on a variety of datasets and found that it significantly boosts the overall accuracy of the model.

The production of top quarks is investigated in proton-nucleus collisions using ATLAS and CMS data, approximately 36.1 inverse microboorns in energy, collected in 2016 at CERN's LHC, where the collider's center-of-mass energy was 5.02 TeV. To identify this production, instead of looking for the usual diphoton signature used in proton-proton collisions, analysts searched for a distinct signature consisting of an isolated electron or muon paired with a bottom quark, represented by a charmed meson or a bottom quark hadron, resulting from the decay of a top quark in proton-nucleus collisions. To validate the detection, researchers used control samples of standard processes: 260 pb^-1 in p+Pb and 18.3 pb^-1 in pp collisions. Statistical analysis detected a 3.3-sigma deviation from background expectations in p+Pb collisions, corresponding to a cross-section of 45 microbarns, along with a measured total cross-section for top quark production exceeding 45 microbarns with a measured total cross-section for top quark production with accompanying minimum bias conditions not exceeding 17.3 nanobarns with a measured total cross-section for top quark production with accompanying minimum bias conditions not exceeding 17.3 nanobarns with accompanying central exclusive production not exceeding 12 nanobarns with a measured total cross-section for top quark production

This study focuses on key elements in text-to-SQL semantic interpretation, specifically identifying columns and their corresponding values. Current methods fall short, particularly when encountering unknown column references. To address this, we propose a new auxiliary task called Column Type Inference and Value Selection, which involves determining column types and selecting relevant values to include in the SQL query. Our auxiliary task has two key components: (1) predicting column types based on existing database information and relevant value content, and (2) identifying values to include in the SQL query from the proposal set. Both of these steps can be optimized through end-to-end training. To further improve performance, we introduce the CTRNet model, which integrates a column type inference module and a value selection module in a multi-task framework. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing single-column approaches and matches multi-column state-of-the-art performance even when columns are known.

The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky to better understand how the large-scale structure of the Universe changes and develops. Although only 1% of the sky is covered in the LoTSS DR1 data release, analysis shows fluctuations that need to be understood. To address this, we created a set of mock surveys based on the LoTAR model by simulating the LoTSS observations. These mocks help scientists analyze the observed sky and separate genuine large-scale structure from noise. Studies confirm that LoTSS sees no significant large-scale structure on more than 400 kiloparsec scales. However, on smaller scales, LoTSS observes a 2.6 power spectrum compared to N-body simulations, possibly indicating an overestimation of noise or an underestimation of the LoTSS by 25%. These findings also show that radio galaxies have a higher density on smaller scales and confirm the concept of galaxy biasing. To summarize, LoTSS observes no significant cosmological structure on large scales or an altered large-scale structure compared to optical surveys using the LoTSS signal as a probe.

This paper introduces an advanced adaptive-sampling algorithm for the High-Dimensional Rank Lasso problem. Our approach utilizes a heuristic-based technique to select relevant data points and update the model parameters, enabling efficient model refinement. By leveraging a sampling-based strategy, we significantly reduce the computational complexity and memory requirements. Furthermore, our algorithm effectively handles large high-dimensional datasets, yielding a reliable and efficient method for solving the HR Lasso problem. Our experimental evaluations demonstrate that the performance of the adaptive-sampling algorithm surpasses state-of-the-art methods, requiring a small fraction of the time and much lower memory resources while achieving a comparable level of accuracy.

For a particle undergoing Brownian motion in a double-well potential under gentle and rapid driving forces, we analyze entropy production using a thermodynamic uncertainty approach. Initially, this method was successful in explaining the phase transition dynamics of some complex systems. In this case, we connect the thermodynamic uncertainty to the entropy change and clarify its relationship with fluctuations in two distinct regimes: one where the particle quickly moves between the wells and another where the particle remains near its minimum. We find that in the rapid, high-temperature regime, the entropy change can be accurately predicted from the force-velocity relationship, an outcome analogous to situation where the particle is in a metastable state. Our analysis also indicates that in the slow, high-temperature regime, the entropy change can be calculated both theoretically and numerically, and that the rate of entropy change is influenced by the amplitude of driving force and the viscosity of the surroundings. We further validate our results by comparing them with numerical simulations involving Monte Carlo methods. Our analysis shows that in a thermally driven system, entropy change can be calculated using the force-velocity relationship, an outcome applicable not only to a metastable state but also to a system experiencing a phase transition.

The beneficial effects of AI on the environment are evident in various solutions such as carbon footprint forecasting, emissions tracking, and climate change modeling. However, these AI-based solutions have concealed environmental impacts necessitating explicit examination. Consequently, several critical issues emerge from the hidden environmental implications of these technologies. Firstly, the AI models' significant energy consumption, produced by processing and data storage, contribute to additional greenhouse gas emissions. Secondly, the reliance on rare and extractively sourced materials for developing AI systems, leading to extraction-related pollution. Thirdly, the influence of AI-driven data exchange on communication infrastructure and resulting electronic pollution. Lastly, the need for proper disposal of retired AI systems to prevent e-waste pollution. Therefore, it is crucial to identify, measure, and mitigate the concealed environmental impacts of AI-based solutions for maximum effectiveness in reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

Prescriptive Process Monitoring, a subcategory of Process Monitoring, relies on predictive analysis to identify the optimal sequence of actions an agent should take at a given process stage to accomplish a desired goal.  The prevalence of Business Process Management Systems and enterprise processes within organizations makes prescriptive process monitoring particularly relevant.  Despite its significance, prescriptive process monitoring remains an underdeveloped field of research.  This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and applications involving prescriptive process monitoring, with a focus on its research history.  Findings are presented in an interactive knowledge base for easy reference.  Drawing from Michel Foucault's concept of 'panopticism,' a conceptual framework is developed to analyze and evaluate prior work, with implications for future research in this domain.

This research introduces an innovative APO error control approach for a nonlinear Boussinesq model that accommodates temperature-dependent heat transfer coefficients and phase transitions within material processing applications. The technique involves developing goal-focused a posteriori estimates for the modeling error and adapting these estimates for goal-oriented adaptive algorithms. To achieve this, a localized error representation is established, requiring the solution of two nonlinear elliptic problems. This approach is implemented in a computational framework for parallel computing on a codeshare basis. The methodology's efficacy is demonstrated through various numerical studies that involve adapting meshes and time-stepping schemes to minimize the modeling error, ultimately resulting in refined solutions that closely resemble exact or heavily discretized reference solutions.

Problems like Combined Bandit Learning and Adversarial Combined Learning, which are variations of the multi-armed combined bandit problem, are being investigated for potential applications in creating more efficient adversarial machine learning models. These problems involve interacting with multiple systems, either online or offline, to gather data, with the goal of developing a unified model that can forecast outcomes from multiple models using collected data. To tackle these challenges, new "kernelization" techniques are being developed to identify key subsets of systems that can help solve the broader problem efficiently. Kernelization refers to a linear reduction in problem size without losing its inherent properties, which in this context, also maintains the problem's optimality. The proposed solutions will demonstrate the development of these kernelization techniques for the identified problems, showcasing their potential for practical use with large datasets.

Building on the fundamental model of structural balance introduced by Heider in 1958, we have combined it with a dynamic opinion-dynamics model, developed by Friedkin and Johnsen in 1999. Our resulting framework, which we call the limited-confidence model, incorporates both individual opinions and social relationships. Under specific conditions, we found that both the social network and individual opinions converge to either an equilibrium state of perfect balance or a stable, oscillating state. Our analysis also involves examining the effects of varying model parameters, such as initial conditions and the manner in which individuals form opinions, on system behavior. Through application of our model to real-world data, we demonstrated its capability to explain and predict human behavior in a realistic scenario.

The theoretical framework for dark stars, which is based on the Einstein-Maxwell-Higgs system, may provide a framework to study dark matter as a gravitational phenomenon resulting from non-linear interactions between gravity, electromagnetism, and dark energy. A specific type of asymptotically flat dark stars, which is related to charged black holes, features a scalar field that causes the scalar field to collapse and give rise to a quasistatic, asymptotically flat solution. Building on this theory, researchers have theoretically confirmed the existence of charged dark matter objects. A recently studied model, which is based on the system described above, has revealed a previously unknown solution to the Einstein-Maxwell-Higgs system, which has led to a better understanding of the interior dynamics of asymptotically flat hairy dark stars. This newly confirmed solution exhibits similar properties to the previously known solution of the Schwarzschild-AntiDeSitter spacetime, which has further highlighted the relationship between the previously known solution and the Schwarzschild-deSitter spacetime. Researchers have also found that the newly confirmed solution could be applicable to the study of a negatively charged dark matter object.

Understanding how cells process genetic information into functional proteins and RNAs, according to temporal cues embedded in chromatin structure, is crucial for elucidating central regulatory processes. Transcription start site selection, influenced by factors like chromatin structure, transcription factors, and RNA interference, involves intricate decisions, potentially delayed due to competing interactions. We introduce a model-based analysis for identifying and characterizing transcription dynamics, particularly suited for studying complex species like Drosa and highly similar species like Mouse and Human. By considering multiple transcription start sites related to each other, the model accounts for co-regulation, reveals patterns of RNA production delays, and identifies slow and fast kinetics of transcription initiation. It also enables comparison across species and identifies evolutionarily conserved transcription dynamics. The model-based analysis provides precise transcription start site identification, surpassing current technologies, and offers insights into the temporal organization of genomes.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where the 0+ and 2+ excited states have different characteristics. It was observed that the 0+ excited states have a solid core with excitation at the 0d-1s and 0g-1s shells, while the 2+ excited states have a core with excitations at the 0d-1s, 0g-1s, and 1h-0f shells. This core-excitation structure is driven by the interaction between particles through a monopole force. It was also discovered that the 0+ and 2+ excited states have different characteristics in terms of how they are arranged and how they are filled, which was not able to be explained through a different theoretical approach. This core-excitation structure is not unique to 64Ni and may be present in other nuclei as well.

Chiral supersymmetric gauge theories, such as SU(N) theories with an N=1 duality, have been a focus for substantial research. Non-supersymmetric versions of these theories, specifically SU(N) QCD3 with an anti-fundamental representation, hold significant interest as they lack known duals and are readily testable with lattice methods. By incorporating a chiral supermultiplet containing a Weyl chiral superfield, we can formulate two non-supersymmetric variants: one with an additional chiral multiplet and another with an anti-chiral multiplet. These variants, represented by $\mathcal{N}=1$ SU(N) QCD3 with an extra chiral superfield and $\mathcal{N}=1$ SU(N) QCD3 with an additional anti-chiral superfield, have unknown duals. However, by employing lattice techniques and introducing a sign structure, we can evaluate and compare lattice observables for both theories to their supersymmetric counterparts. Notably, we can relate both non-supersymmetric theories to a free theory via a solvable model, providing further insight into their behavior.

A linear complementary pair of group codes $(C, D)$ is formed when the direct sum of $C$ and $D$ results in the entire group algebra $R$. This concept extends the idea of a complementary pair of group codes. In this paper, we establish criteria under which a linear complementary pair of group codes can be obtained from a group code $C$, using a unique divisor ring $R$ based on a finite primary ideal. This finding is further supported by several examples.

We introduce "bucket tables," a simple, compact data structure that enables faster exact computation for simplified representations of Markov decision process (MDP) models. MDP models emerge from graphical models with both state and decision variables. By utilizing a bucket table, which organically emerges during the algorithmic process, we can speed up the machine learning-based efficient exact solution generation for the most critical regions of MDP models, which in turn facilitates faster overall solution generation. We incorporate this innovation into the existing Maximum Partition Entropy (MPE) solver, enhancing its efficiency. Moreover, we integrate this new data structure into two cutting-edge MPE-based optimization methods to provide an efficient and improved version for solving constrained optimization problems in graphical models.

Human attention span is drawn to visual stimuli, making visual information highly accessible. Yet, in daily life, important information often passes visual detection and relies on auditory input. Integrating multiple sensory inputs enhances information processing, particularly in complex situations involving both visual and auditory cues. In this research, we address the challenge of identifying fallen items in a shopping cart by merging asynchronous audio-visual information. An audio-visual detector was created and trained on a shopping cart filled with common household items, producing both audio and visual signals. To accommodate asynchronous integration, a designated module was designed, allowing the combination of pre-recorded shopping cart sounds with real-time visual images of falling items. An asynchronous multi-modal neural network was implemented, tested with synthetic data, and demonstrated effectiveness in its proposed method.

Shear thickening transitions are rare events in highly viscous fluids that become even more viscous when subjected to rapid and intense shear forces. Despite their unusual characteristics, these transitions have been identified in various forms of soft matter, often triggering massive and sudden increases in the flow rate and viscosity of a substance. Due to their energetic and dynamic implications, it is crucial to understand the universal properties of these transitions; however, the limited availability of high-quality experimental data has hindered progress in this field. To address this limitation, we have collected a large dataset of shear thickening measurements for multiple types of soft matter, employing a novel experimental approach that ensures accuracy and sensitivity. By analyzing this comprehensive dataset, we have discovered a universal relationship between the flow rate and viscosity changes during shear thickening, applicable across various substances and scenarios. Moreover, our findings can be rationalized using a simplified hydrodynamic model that takes into account factors like the distribution of shear thickening events, their rapidity, and the associated increase in the fluid's internal pressure. The combination of our experimental work and hydrodynamic modeling provides a foundation for further research into the shear thickening phenomenon and its general properties.

This study investigates hourly electricity consumption patterns in Ghana's greatest metropolitan area, Accra, specifically during the period of severe power shortages in 2015. To gain insights into these patterns, the study employs advanced Markov switching models, combining data-driven and machine learning approaches to identify any underlying trends or cycles in the data. Among various candidate models, the most suitable was the AR(2)-MS-AR(1)-GA model, showcasing exceptional accuracy and outperforming other models in this study through superior LIC and AIC metrics. Valuable insights from this model include the identification of distinct states in electricity consumption patterns, along with the probability of transitioning between these states and forecasting future usage. Notably, the study finds that average hourly electricity consumption in Accra exhibits diurnal and weekly patterns but no evident seasonal trend. These patterns are in line with prior studies on other countries. The study suggests that incorporating knowledge of specific events, such as power shortages, could further enhance model performance.

The objective of this study was to quantify the extent of personalization in Google's Web search and its implications. We discovered that the majority of Web search users are personalizing their searches without realizing it. A non-personalized Google search revealed that up to 15% of the top ten search results are tailored to individual users. Conducting four independent experiments demonstrated that as many as 17% of search queries are modified to reflect users' browsing history. A significant concern arising from these findings was the potential for personalizers to miss relevant information. Employing a method to assess the extent of missed relevance, we found that personalizers may overlook between 6% and 14% of relevant content.

This study introduces an advanced neural network called GRCNN, designed to recognize graph structures, and trains it to accurately interpret flow charts and produce corresponding computer code. GRCNN is essentially a combination of a flow chart diagram network and a program generator network working in tandem. The network's spatial perception abilities allow it to identify individual elements within a flow chart, while its sequential processing capability enables it to incorporate temporal relationships between these elements. The network's fundamental task is to link input nodes in a flow chart with corresponding output program elements, so a program can be synthesized by feeding real-world data through this transformation. To achieve this, GRCNN is optimized using a novel loss function that measures similarity between program elements, and is further refined by comparing predicted programs with actual code from a large dataset, and evaluating performance using metrics such as accuracy, precision, and recall. The results show that GRCNN surpasses earlier techniques with high accuracy, suggesting a promising approach to graph structure recognition and program generation.

This text explores various reduction techniques that aid climate scientists in navigating complex high-dimensional systems. It distills these methods into three primary categories: physical, statistical, and dynamical reductions, before delving into a detailed examination of each type of reduction. The goal is to provide readers with an in-depth understanding of each technique, exemplified through recently published studies in the Journal of Climate, Dynamics, and Atmospheres.

The development of kilonova ejecta through the interaction of the r-process elements provides valuable insights into the nucleosynthesis occurring after a binary neutron star merger. To better understand these elements, we have carried out a relativistic atomic structure calculation for the Os-like sequence and obtained the energy levels, wavefunctions, and alignment patterns for Os, Ir, Pt, Au, Hg, and Tl using the relativistic atomic structure code, GRASP0. The findings from these calculations were then combined with the existing work to create a comprehensive set of relativistic atomic data that spans up to atomic number 207. This data was then utilized to model the behavior of Ir, Pt, and Au using the relativistic atomic structure code, MOTA, and was then compared with the existing data in the NIST Atomic Physics Format to obtain the opacity tables for these elements, which were then made available online through the Chalk River Atomic Data and Nuclear Data Project. These tables, which cover energies up to 10 million electron volts, were based on the relativistic atomic structure model and were specifically designed to model the behavior of the metals in a relativistic context. They also include the ground and excited state configurations for the ions, as well as their position-dependent energy levels, and alignment patterns, which are critical for understanding the behavior of these metals in a relativistic context. Additionally, we used these atomic data and opacity tables to model the synthetic spectra of the post-merger environment of binary neutron star

Deep learning-based segmentation of the gastrointestinal region is crucial for automated assessment of gastrointestinal diseases and image content. This is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process, but with the rising power of computational capabilities, it has become more feasible. Our research leverages a modified U-Net model to segment the gastrointestinal region, and we evaluate this approach using the MICCAI 2015 CHISTOPIA Challenge dataset consisting of 300 videos. This dataset poses significant challenges due to varied imaging modalities, low resolution, and a complex gastrointestinal region. Our proposed method effectively segments the gastrointestinal region, demonstrating superiority over existing techniques with an segmentation score of 0.75, compared to the best previous method score of 0.67.

Compositional data analysis requires a thorough understanding of the mathematical and graphical representations specific to this field. Although important, this topic is often overlooked in the existing literature. To bridge this gap, this tutorial provides a comprehensive overview of the key concepts, leveraging the R programming language to illustrate complex linear algebra through interactive visualizations. We cover the fundamental ideas of compositional data, focus on the Kalis-Barnes-Cressie matrix, and demonstrate how the matrix's eigenvectors and eigenvalues relate to the CCA coordinates, offering a fresh perspective on this concept. Furthermore, we examine common data visualization techniques used in the field and their implications on interpretation.

Past research has suggested that sub-Saturn mass exoplanets might be rare around their host stars due to various formation mechanisms that smooth out distributions of planetary masses and orbits. However, this study aims to explore the planet population around late-type stars using a comprehensive, high-sensitivity exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS observations. By leveraging detailed analysis of the CORALIE/HARPS data and a proven statistical approach, researchers discover that sub-Saturn mass exoplanets are more abundant than previously expected. Notably, early findings from this study initially indicated lower frequencies of sub-Saturn mass exoplanets compared to hot Jupiters, but further investigation using a more stringent selection of late-type host stars reveals the opposite: sub-Saturn mass exoplanets are indeed more common than hot Jupiters. These results challenge the idea that there needs to be a 'wasteland' of sub-planetary mass objects missing in the sample, and instead suggest that exoplanets can naturally extend from terrestrial to Jovian masses within a given temperature range.

In the field of autonomous systems, attention mechanisms allow for controlled filtering of sensory input, but current models are hindered by their lack of robustness to unexpected system disruptions. This limitation could be addressed by drawing on insights from optimal reinforcement learning, which seeks to exploit novel opportunities by exploring their link to information gain. This connection suggests that maximizing mutual information between sensory inputs and system states could enable the development of more resilient attention models. This paper introduces such an approach, where a shared latent variable is used to increase its own value between inputs and states, thus leading to the creation of robust attention models. Experiments with simulated vehicles in variable environments have demonstrated the effectiveness of this method.

The compressed mass spectrum in the dark matter sector, a characteristic of certain models including the Wess-Zumino model and its extensions, is a natural outcome, in which the masses of the dark matter fields are relatively close. By investigating the Yukawa interaction between a fermionic dark matter particle and a bosonic dark matter particle, we have found that the Yukawa coupling can be constrained. In the context of compressed mass spectra, this interaction gives rise to distinct, observable recombination features in the kinetic equilibrium of the dark matter particles. Specifically, for the case of a fermionic and bosonic dark matter particle with masses near each other, but not equal, the Yukawa interaction can result in an early onset of dark matter particle decay, potentially leading to observable deviations in the Planck satellite data and upcoming experiments like COBE, MAP, and CMBPol.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, mirroring brain circuit behaviors, albeit with limited applicability due to large training demands and memory needs. Brain structures pose constraints such as synaptic distance costs and thus sparsity, resulting in local connectivity patterns. This study presents a trainable, grid-based sparsified RNN (gRNN) with an inherent neural architecture resembling the brain's wire layout and demonstrates its capability to solve a wide range of tasks efficiently. The results show that gRNN outperforms traditional full RNNs on various cognitive tasks like navigation, navigation with cues, navigation with memory, and value-guided reinforcement learning tasks, requiring significantly fewer training attempts and neural parameter adjustments. The research further explores gRNN's structural properties and suggests its potential as a basic brain module for more sophisticated neural network designs, potentially mimicking the brain's neural circuit mechanisms.

Researchers initially developed the geometric categority of finitely generated algebras in the late 1990s. This non-computational approach was initially applied to commutative algebras and was later expanded to associative and Lie algebras independently. Subsequent work generalized the concept to nilpotent algebras over a field with a specific characteristic and, further, to any commutative ring. This formalism is based on transforming the algebra into a polynomial ring over the given base ring, followed by categorizing it via the resulting scheme. This study presents a comprehensive overview of the geometric categority for nilpotent algebras, also addressing questions related to the structure theorem, presentations, and free algebras within specific constraints.

Active galactic nuclei are among the brightest objects in the universe, outshining all other light from distant galaxies. Their powerful beams, traveling at the speed of light, emit radiation across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, spanning from radio waves to gamma rays. This radiation, covering the entire spectrum, enables researchers to simulate how matter moves through the environment of these beams, creating complex patterns in the shape of loops or rings. These synthetic observations help scientists visualize the impact of various factors on the appearance of these beams, such as the alignment of the black hole and the plane of the disk, as well as how matter in the environment of the beams scatters light. This research investigates how the scattering of light in the direction of the observer, caused by the simulation of large-scale structures in the environment of the beams, affects the appearance of AGNs at the highest redshifts, primarily by blocking the signal in the radio and X-ray ranges. This research specifically examines the scattering of X-rays and radio waves at redshifts of 6 and 7, focusing particularly on the change in appearance when the angle of the observer and the black hole changes, as well as how the scattering of light in the direction of the observer affects the appearance of AGNs when the angle of the observer changes. This research draws on existing studies of the CMB and radio waves from nearby galaxies, using theoretical simulations to analyze the influence of structures in the environment of the beams on the appearance of these beams. The paper explores the possibilities for Lagrangians representing non-kinetic, spherically symmetric gravitational fields. It is established that variable gravitational mass $M$, based on distance, is a characteristic of kinematic Lagrangians. In contrast, the scalar curvature theory $\mathcal{R}$, when combined with a cosmological constant $\Lambda$, offers a viable option for describing static, external gravitational fields. Additionally, the paper examines the general relativistic rotation equations and assesses the potential of the scalar curvature theory $\mathcal{R}$, supplemented with a cosmological constant $\Lambda$, to describe gravitational potentials observed in the solar system.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image contrast.  The proposed descriptor includes a binary feature that distinguishes between the sign of the Laplacian operator's results applied to image data and reversed image data.  This descriptor, included in the enhanced 3D Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (3D SIFT), was used to develop a feature-based point-to-point registration algorithm for 3D image volumes.  Experiments demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed method involve registering MRI scans of human brains and 3D scanning data of pottery items.  Comparisons with established image registration techniques, such as ITK-SNAP, show that the proposed method outperforms these methods in terms of accuracy and robustness.

We've examined the light curves of a unique astrophysical phenomenon, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, an esteemed member of the GJ 1655 ab system. This rare binary consists of two ancient stars on the verge of merging, characterized by a 40.5-minute orbital period. Our detailed analysis involves studying the variations in optical and near-infrared light as they relate to the moving components of the stars. 

Our observations reveal that in addition to the expected 40.5 minutes cycle, there is an inherent pattern of 802 minutes present in all the examined data. It's worth noting that this secondary cycle is prominent in the data obtained during 2016-2017, but it's absent in the 2017-2018 measurements. 

Our predictions suggest that this secondary cycle is most likely the result of irregular variations in the shape of the secondary star, caused by the ongoing accumulation of material transferred from one star to another. As a result, the secondary cycle becomes harder to recognize as the contact points between the stars become less distinct. 

During the 2016-2017 cycle, the contact points align with the secondary cycle, but in the 2017-2018 cycle, they align with the primary 40.5-minute orbit. It's also possible that the observed secondary cycle is actually the result of uneven surface patterns on one of the stars, but this would mean the secondary cycle is not connected to the primary orbit.

In deep learning models, the majority of components receive backpropagation updates, except for those that utilize the global average pooling operation.  This paper demonstrates that poolable components can be expanded to encompass neural networks employing optimal transport-based pooling methods like max pooling and average pooling, with corresponding backpropagation updates.  A new, more general framework for differentiable pooling is then established, enabling the seamless incorporation of various pooling methods.  This breakthrough enables the use of higher-order pooling in neural networks, enhancing their performance.

This research presents the findings of the host galaxies for a comprehensive set of active galactic nuclei, which have been categorized into four classes based on their spectral characteristics. By utilizing archival Chandra data, we investigated the X-ray properties of 69 AGN, identifying significant variations between the distinct AGN types in terms of their location, luminosity, hard-to-soft ratio, and absorption. Notably, two AGN types, classified as 'Steep' and 'Flat', exhibit differences in their X-ray hard-to-soft spectrum, while 'Steep' sources display softer spectra at higher energies. Conversely, sources labeled as 'Variable' and 'High-Variable', show no distinct differences in their X-ray properties. Employing multivariate analysis, we have identified the significant factors influencing the differences in hard X-ray luminosity and photon index, which are the orientation of the jets (with an importance of 56% or higher) and nuclear activity (with an importance of 30% or higher), as well as the presence of a collimated jet in the case of hard X-rays. By constructing rest-frame hard X-ray to ultraviolet spectral energy distributions for 19 sources, we have observed that the P-AH trend is reversed, indicating that the UV power is greater than the hard X-ray power. This research paper confirms that a particular flat rotational surface in a four-dimensional Euclidean space is unique and relies on a singular Gaussian map being 1-type.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable amount of annotated data, and previously, pre-training on PASCAL Object Classess was shown to be beneficial with labeled data from the Cat-200 dataset. Our investigation found that using the Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) task for pre-training resulted in improved performance on PASCAL and Cat-200, and also required less annotated data for fine-tuning compared to traditional pre-training methods. MDE's pre-training benefits translate to reduced annotation costs during the neural network's training process.

Generating narratives about time-series data is crucial in various fields, 
enabling the creation of engaging stories for analytics, sales, and marketing 
purposes. However, creating narratives that accurately describe complex 
time-series data while maintaining analytical and business relevance is highly 
challenging, particularly when involving the incorporation of contextual 
descriptions. Currently available methods are limited, requiring pre-defined 
templates or descriptions that fail to adapt to dynamic market conditions 
and result in narratives lacking natural flow and context. To address this, 
we introduce TCube, a neural time-series narration system capable of adapting 
to various domains while ensuring coherence and relevance. By employing a 
description generator trained on time-series data, TCube is able to produce 
descriptions that incorporate time-series-specific terms, such as "upward 
trends" and "peak periods," while also using contextual descriptions to enhance 
narratives. To facilitate domain neutrality, we developed a Domain-Neutral 
Description Generator (DNDG), which can describe any given time-series using 
domain-neutral terms. To assess its effectiveness, we conducted user studies, 
submitting TCube-generated narratives to users who demonstrated familiarity 
with the domain, resulting in TCube being preferred over baseline systems in 
all cases. Furthermore, TCube's efficacy was validated through its adoption 
by leading technology and entertainment companies.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved significant discoveries involving CP violation and rare decays of B mesons. This study reviews two key findings: the measurement of CP-violating phase in $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the observation of the $B^0_s \to \phi \mu^+\mu^-$ process. These discoveries contribute crucial data towards understanding CKM unitarity and enabling more precise predictions of theoretical models.

On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model with the basic interaction and an external stress represented by the interaction with a heat bath at a finite temperature. We demonstrate the existence of new periodic states, which are distinct from the well-known ferromagnetic and paramagnetic states, in the vicinity of the zero-temperature transition point. These periodic states, characterized by a relatively prime number of spins, exhibit unique properties and can be stabilized through a specific choice of temperature and external stress.

This study investigates the global well-posedness of certain nonlinear hyperbolic partial differential equations with time sublogarithmic coefficients. By establishing an energy estimate that is relatively stable and can be controlled, we resolve issues related to the energy's rapid initial increase. Notably, our proof adheres to the letter to the pioneering work of Christodoulou-Taylor on the Lorentzian metric.

This research explores the application of a specific type of Recurrent Neural Network, known as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), in tackling the challenge of Japanese term segmentation. Since LSTM models can effectively capture long-term dependencies in data, this study aims to leverage that capability. Using a character-based approach, where each character is a discrete unit, the experiment trains an LSTM model on a dataset consisting of annotated Japanese terms. To evaluate its performance, the model's predictions are compared to the actual segmentation labels. Notably, this study's results demonstrate that an LSTM model trained solely on characters achieves segmentation accuracy comparable to models trained on more traditional features, such as morphological and phonological attributes.

External web links on Stack Overflow can significantly enhance users' understanding of software challenges, projects, and methodologies by providing access to relevant information outside the platform.  To expand the scope of knowledge available within the SO community, we conducted an investigation into the most frequently shared external web links on Stack Overflow.  By analyzing a dataset of 359,880 questions containing 543,720 external web links, our analysis revealed a substantial portion of these links (74.67%) are still accessible, with a significant percentage (16.44%) leading to their own Stack Overflow questions.  Further, we identified over half of the most popular shared links (57.14%) comprise external web links initially shared within the top 10% most popular Stack Overflow questions.  By examining frequently shared external web links, we gained insights into SO users' collaboration and knowledge management practices, as well as the extent to which they contribute to knowledge aggregation and distribution across the platform.  Ultimately, our research may inspire the development of new features or functionalities that facilitate knowledge aggregation and facilitate the aggregation of knowledge on Stack Overflow.

Galactic diversity in science fiction has been a subject of discussion for fans and scholars, with a significant portion of fictional galaxies resembling Earth, and the majority of the remaining galaxies being benign in their environments. This study aims to understand the reasons behind this diversity, and it offers a simplified theoretical model to explain the prevalence of Earth-like and benign galaxies. A crucial aspect of this paper is a comparison of the number of galaxies in the Milky Way that are similar to our own and those that are not, and the same for the Andromeda Galaxy. This comparison yields an answer to the question of how many fictional galaxies in each category might be present. Additionally, the paper explores potential explanations for the abundance of benign galaxies in fiction.

Achieving significant global climate change mitigation involves cooperative actions from multiple nations, which necessitates effective communication among policymakers and climate experts. To facilitate meaningful discussions, we suggest integrating a climate knowledge base into climate negotiation processes. This knowledge base will serve as a reference point for relevant climate science, technological advancements, and policy examples. By accessing this information, negotiation participants can gain insights into best practices, demonstrate the implications of their actions, and explore potential solutions. To demonstrate its utility, we develop a graphical interface illustrating the structure of a negotiation and highlight the potential benefits of incorporating the knowledge base. Furthermore, we investigate methods for updating the knowledge base through the analysis of negotiation documents. Establishing and refining this knowledge base depends on the collaborative input of climate experts who will contribute, evaluate, and refine the knowledge base throughout the negotiation process.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using various models, trained on diverse patient datasets, to extract symptoms and their relationships.
Our research tested whether models trained on different groups of patients, selected based on factors like age and health conditions, could also accurately identify symptoms and their connections in other groups.
The outcome showed that while the models performed similarly within the groups they were trained on, they showed little improvement when applied to new, unrelated groups.
This suggests that currently available data is enough to perfectly identify symptoms and their connections for patients with similar characteristics.
Moreover, our findings indicate that models can equally excel on datasets from different hospitals, despite being trained on a specific hospital's data.
Our study paves the way for further research on whether these models can also accurately identify more complex relationships between symptoms and their connections.

Deep reinforcement learning has gained significant attention in the field of autonomous driving due to its capability to learn from environmental interactions and adapt to various scenarios. The process involves an agent's interaction with the driverless car, received sensory input from multiple cameras and sensors, and navigation within a structured environment governed by rules. The objective is to attain consecutive rewards, and as a result, maximize the total reward over time. The system's efficiency relies on the balance between exploration and exploitation, and overcoming challenges such as spatiotemporal dependencies, missing sensor data, and diverse road user behaviors to achieve high-level autonomy.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models has been hindered by their enormous computational requirements for both initial training and real-time operation. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has been presented as a potential solution to these problems. This study presents an efficient classification task solver that combines the precision of digital systems with the energy-efficiency of analog ones through the use of random neural networks composed of simple threshold units. We provide accurate descriptions of the model's parameters, clear evaluation criteria, and detailed simulation protocols that allow for replication of our results. The study demonstrates that binary RNNs can achieve outstanding energy-efficiency at relatively low error rates, surpassing performance of more complex hybrd CNNs both in terms of energy consumption and processing speed.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark stars under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature. We have derived the equation of state for spin-polarized quark stars using the MIT bag model, where the effective mass of quarks is influenced by magnetic field strength and temperature, and also considering the effect of magnetic flux at the quark star's surface. We further examined the behavior of negative charged quark stars in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and plotted temperature against specific heat, adiabatic mass, and entropy, respectively. Additionally, we have tabulated these properties at various temperatures and studied the behavior of quark star's surface with respect to magnetic field strength.

Pando, an innovative computational engine, enables the creation of Browser Extensions that can run highly interactive and dynamic Browser-based Personal Assistants, taking input from users through interactions such as tabs, searches, voice prompts, and hotkeys, and producing output as notifications, visuals, and rich media. Pando boasts a comprehensive set of features, encompassing natural language processing, sophisticated search, tab management, data storage, and notification systems, as well as a user-friendly storage service powered by GraphQL for seamless data management between extensions and web applications. With its broad range of capabilities, Pando empowers the development of Browser-based Personal Assistants that can execute intricate workflows and tasks, such as managing multiple tabs to interact with various web applications, executing voice commands, and performing voice-driven data entry, among many other features.

A new nonparametric approach for estimating nonlinear eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix has been developed. This method involves minimizing a criterion function that facilitates straightforward gradient descent optimization. As a result, the estimator's asymptotic behavior can be analyzed using statistical smoothing principle techniques. Our study demonstrates that the estimator's statistical efficiency is comparable to that of an ideal parametric estimator designed from the asymptotic curve geometry. To validate the efficiency of the proposed estimator, a simulation study has been conducted, showing that its behavior closely mimics that of the ideal parametric estimator in various scenarios.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a gap. Specifically, we show that these transformations share the same family of attracting Cantor sets and have isomorphic Hausdorff measures under certain conditions. Our analysis also establishes the validity of the six-fold conjecture proposed by Aaronson and Brisebarre.

We've found that gauge theories with $SO(N_{c})$ as a gauge group and matter fields represented as vectors confine, resulting from monopole condensation and the quark bilinear breaking $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry down to $SO(N_{F})$. Our findings derive from an ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric theory, specifically with anomaly-mediated supersymmetry breaking.

Machine learning models such as random forests and boosted trees have proven effective across various fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. By incorporating a disentanglement method from the neural network field, we propose a new tool to improve the interpretability of these models. Initially, we demonstrate the application of this method to traditional gradient tree boosting models. To make the approach more practical, we also develop a way to efficiently apply it to large datasets. Furthermore, we introduce a way to generate visual representations of variable importance that are easy to understand and order. Through testing on artificial and real-world data, we show that the method reveals statistically significant and reproducible patterns in attribute importance. Additionally, we found that our approach aligns with the original variable importance output from BRT models, but it provides more precise and reliable results.

Federated learning allows multiple entities to collaborate on model training while maintaining their data's confidentiality, as the training process occurs on their local systems. Despite this advantage, the efficiency of the training process is hindered by communication limitations, as periodic model exchange requires entities to reveal their local update vectors. To overcome this issue, we've devised an approach continuing from prior research to facilitate training across diverse computation environments, encompassing cloud, edge, and remote setups, through a reliable and efficient gradient sharing protocol. This method replaces the need for direct model exchange with secure, encrypted gradient uploads, enabling entities to collaborate on training without compromising their data's security or system's performance.

Self-driving vehicles rely heavily on powerful computers capable of processing complex algorithms in real-time. However, this real-time processing capability comes with a significant drawback: the need for expensive and bulky hardware. This paper presents a novel approach to overcome this limitation by shifting the computational load to external devices. A lightweight embedded system connected to a vehicle issues basic driving commands, receiving video footage and sensor data from external units. This connection allows multiple drivers to share their capabilities, enabling the vehicle to adapt and improve performance through their combined efforts. We demonstrate the efficiency of this model by comparing traditional approaches to autonomous driving, showing that this setup results in a substantial reduction in processing demands. This breakthrough enables autonomous driving operations on more affordable and portable embedded platforms, opening doors to new possibilities such as autonomous shuttles and other small-scale applications.

This research introduces a novel approach for automating system call filtering in containerized microservices. A 'timeloop' is a machine learning-based controller that learns the system call patterns required by each individual service and enables accurate identification of unnecessary system calls. This is accomplished through a training process that leverages a controlled environment to create a profile of expected system calls for each service, thereby enabling the timeloop to efficiently identify and block unnecessary system calls in real-time. By comparing different training methods and evaluating the performance of various machine learning algorithms, our study demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of using a timeloop to improve the security of containerized microservices by minimizing the risk of malicious system calls.

Merchandise space forms provide a useful framework for modeling consumer behavior in retail settings, enabling researchers to investigate topics like customer engagement with products in physical spaces. This paper explores linear classifiers applied to merchandise space forms, which offer several benefits, including reduced computational complexity and more interpretable decisions. Linear classifiers can also leverage existing libraries and take advantage of specialized hardware, such as GPUs, for faster training and inference. To illustrate the application, the authors conduct a case study using merchandise space form models of two different retail contexts.

Despite numerous studies on the stellar population around a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy, the fundamental distribution laws of these stars remain unclear due to limitations in observing techniques and theoretical models. Using a customized grid search approach and a large database of stellar masses and orbital energies, we re-explore the stellar population and find that the mass and energy distributions of the stellar population can be accurately represented as power laws, specifically a sequence of N populations with exponents of $\alpha_i$, given that the cumulative mass distribution function is defined as $f(M)\propto dN/dM \proti^{N-1}$ and the cumulative energy distribution function is defined as $f(E)\propto dN/dE \proti^{N-1}$. We show that the mass and energy distributions are independent of each other and that each population's exponent can be determined based on the average mass and energy of the population, the total mass of the population, and the orbital velocity at a specific radius, ultimately revealing how these distributions are interconnected and influenced by the supermassive black hole's gravity.

This introduction focuses on random model predictive control, a methodological framework that facilitates the use of probabilistic models in closed-loop control systems. It is notable that probabilistic models are increasingly employed in fields such as systems monitoring and adjustment, control system design, and resource allocation, due to their capability of handling uncertainty in a concise manner. Nonetheless, existing model predictive control methods are typically grounded in certain, knowable information, whereas probabilistic models are often based on uncertain knowledge. Consequently, there is a pressing need to develop methods that leverage probabilistic models in control systems. 

We propose a sequence of steps to establish a method for random model predictive control. Initially, we define key terms and establish relationships between probabilistic sets and sets of certain events. Next, we formulate an optimal control problem using probabilistic models, followed by a methodological framework for enforcing feasibility and tracking objectives in closed-loop systems. 

For illustration purposes, a simulation example is presented that highlights the practical significance of utilizing probabilistic models in control systems. Furthermore, a numerical example is included to demonstrate the practical implications of employing probabilistic models in closed-loop systems.

This paper introduces a novel technique for recovering high-dimensional vectors from low-dimensional factors in the presence of ambient noise, using a small number of measurements. Building on Singular Component Analysis, our approach is grounded in the principles of compressive sensing, which reaffirms the importance of working directly with incomplete data. The development of an optimization-based framework for Compressive Singular Component Analysis reveals that its performance limits can be described in terms of the characteristics of the underlying singular vectors. Consequently, existing methods can be reevaluated in light of this new perspective, and algorithms like Compressive Principal Component Analysis and Randomized Singular Value Decomposition are shown to achieve these performance limits under certain conditions. Furthermore, our investigation leads to the design of an iterative algorithm, which utilizes partial data and is capable of extracting low-dimensional components at a cost proportional to the number of measurements. Empirical tests have demonstrated the efficacy of this algorithm in recovering low-dimensional structures present in various real-world datasets.

A versatile dynamical model, the Gurtin-MacKay model, has been expanded to include random fluctuations, resulting in a chaotic behavior caused by interactions between species competing for limited resources, such as habitat or food. This expansion leads to two main outcomes: (1) all species eventually disappear due to overwhelming noise, or (2) multiple species coexist in a stable equilibrium. We have developed formulas for the maximum number of coexisting species, determined by model parameters, and the conditions under which any given number of coexisting species is achievable, dependent on species' mean population sizes. Our analysis involves a species' fundamental 'colonization ability' and the 'competition intensity' when thriving, which contradict each other, representing the core conflict species must balance to survive.

We investigate the category of local von Neumann algebras within the context of abelian quantum double models. By proving that the interplay of compact regions and braiding effects results in a monoidal category, we establish that the quantum field associated with these models is a well-structured, symmetric monoidal category. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the restriction to the algebra of compactly local observables forms a subcategory. Notably, our findings provide a formal description of the phase structure within these models, allowing for the classification of phases by the tensor categories arising from different irreducible subfactors. Our research also confirms that the phase structure is invariant under mild adjustments to the models. We also show that the models featuring a non-degenerate Hamiltonian that arises from the combination of a bounded region's density matrix and the relative density matrix are phase-unique. Our analysis is accompanied by a concise summary of known results on extended quantum systems that are derived from abelian quantum double models.

A coherent feedback loop connects the single-magnon double-well and double-cavity systems, enabling the exchange of magnons and photons. This configuration enables efficient generation of hybrid Tonks-Greenberger states, which occur when magnons and phonons become entangled with photons. However, this exchange also introduces decoherence that negatively impacts the formation of such states. Yet, by adjusting key parameters - frequency detuning, phonon decay rate, and fluid driving strength - optimal conditions can be achieved to maximize entanglement. We explored this possibility and confirmed that considerable levels of entanglement can indeed be attained. Ultimately, the strongest hybrid Tonks-Greenberg states can be produced with the fastest decaying phonons and largest frequency imbalances.

We've completed a thorough compilation of one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for QCD, using a dimensionally-regularized framework. Our work builds upon previous research and employs an effective technique to remove spurious divergences, allowing us to derive exact expressions for all relevant splitting operators. We've specifically obtained precise predictions for all pairs of different partons in this context. Additionally, we've validated our results against various one-loop processes and can verify their correctness through direct calculations. We believe that the obtained expressions will be very useful for creating customized parton-shower codes and will likely have significant applications in creating higher-order predictions for large-scale processes like Hadron Collider experiments.

A comprehensive proof of the Neron desingularization (Neron resolution) theorem is presented for one-dimensional local rings, with an explicit construction of the normalized base change morphism, demonstrating that the morphism is topologically of finite presentation (topologically quasi-finite) if and only if the corresponding map on spectra is open.

For thousands of years, people have relied on sundials as primary sources for horology, using the sun's shadow to track time. This ancient clock was particularly significant in ancient Greek and Roman cultures. In line with the 13th International Conference on the History of Science, our project 'Suryakala' aims to document historical sundials in Indonesia. With a team of researchers from various disciplines, we have been conducting a comprehensive survey of sundials across the country, combining field measurements and computational modeling to verify their accuracy. This effort not only preserves Indonesia's rich cultural heritage but also educates students and researchers about the ancient art of creating functional sundials. Our website features a public database with detailed sundial records, as well as interactive tools and educational resources. This project also includes hands-on activities for students to create their own sundials using different methods and materials. With a mobile app, we have made it easy for anyone to quickly set up a sundial and verify its accuracy using their smartphone's GPS and camera. Our app allows users to take photos of the sundial, calculate the local time, and compare it to standard time. This process also generates a unique QR code that can be scanned to access additional features and information. Our website and app offer a range of functions to manage and share sundial data, from recording and verifying device performance to sharing photos and receiving notifications of nearby sundials. With a comprehensive database and just one year of operation, our Suryakala project

In future cognitive networks, coexisting D2D communication and surface-to-air reconfigurable reflectors will be integral components. This network optimizes energy efficiency by leveraging D2D communication and surface reflection. We focus on introducing a new surface-based cognitive approach that allows a common shared channel among D2D nodes and surface reflections, while guaranteeing reliable and efficient communication. This approach implements a surface-level noncooperative game to determine the optimal number of reflections and D2D node pairs through Nash equilibria. Furthermore, a new surface-based integral metric measures the integrated data and energy transfer capabilities. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method achieves efficient and reliable communication, while increasing overall network performance by adjusting the number of reflections.

The pandemic-driven shortage of LDV systems has highlighted the need to utilize a single LDV system to obtain two-dimensional velocity measurements in diverse applications. This paper explores the effectiveness of dividing the measurement volume into two separate regions, enabling the simultaneous collection of independent measurements in a side-by-side configuration. Different operational techniques have been proposed for each area. The paper concentrates on refining particle image velocimetry, a proven technique for acquiring full-field velocity data, by optimizing its functional parameters, such as the number of images, processing iterations, and spatial resolution. The proposed method aims to obtain 2D velocity profiles with high spatial resolution, precise velocity data, and minimal noise in both turbulent and solid flows. The proposed approach has been validated in both numerical and experimental settings.

Bull, Kuhn, and Seldin introduced a fundamental challenge to early logical theory, demonstrating that Kripke's semantic framework for normal modal logic was not based on a sound logical axiomatization. In this paper, we explore a general approach to linguistic expression analysis and apply it to evaluate the validity of certain logical arguments involving binary relations. This methodology enables us to define a notion of logical validity and to express this notion in terms of a corresponding notion of satisfaction, thereby reversing Bull et al.'s argument and establishing a sound logical axiomatization for normal modal logic based on a first-order language with binary relations.

A programmable phase plate (PPP) can produce the same image modulation as a conventional phase plate (CP) through controlled thinning of electron beams. Our study explores the possibilities of PPPs replacing phase plates that require manual precession and correcting spherical aberration in transmission electron microscopes. We found that a PPP with an effective aperture can perform these functions, but may not correct all forms of aberrations. The advantages and limitations of PPPs were scrutinized to determine their suitability for various applications.

This paper explores the interconnectedness of computational assessments and the fundamental nature of computation, delving into the core characteristics of computability theory to clarify a key concept. A step-by-step breakdown of what constitutes a computational assessment, followed by a step-by-step evaluation process, reveals how each computational step can be likened to a basic logical operation, underscoring the fact that assessment computation shares the same core principles as general computation. To illustrate this connection, the paper adapts iconic models from the history of computation, reinterpreting them within the context of assessment computation. As a result, the paper demonstrates how the property of termination applies universally to all computational assessments, making it a universally applicable metric for measuring computation everywhere.
This note seeks to enumerate the possible locations of a random walk in a d-dimensional cube under a specific distance metric, and we successfully generalize a prior finding to achieve this goal.

Building upon earlier research by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin, we have successfully generalized their findings to a broader class of spacetimes, defining the structure of the resulting polymer-induced spacetime. Following this, we examined the quasinormal mode problem in this expanded spacetime, and calculated the corresponding spectrum of the scalar, vector, and gravitational fields.

Heat conduction within doped graphene, shaped as monolayer and bilayer flakes with various layouts, is studied using theoretical methods. All calculations consider thermal interactions among charge carriers, assuming the thermal energy is contained within the systems. This research investigates the influence of coupling between graphene and phonons on heat conduction in doped graphene bilayers. An alternative approach is used to model this interaction, which involves expressing it as a weak perturbation. In monolayer graphene, phonons have a minimal effect on transport, which is dominated by charge carriers. In bilayers, however, coupling between graphene and phonons and electron-phonon interactions have significant effects on transport, which is further influenced by parameters such as layer spacing, orientation, and doping levels. These parameters also determine whether charge carriers or phonons contribute most to heat conduction. This knowledge could facilitate the optimization of bilayer graphene's thermal properties.

Neural text-to-speech (NTS) systems can generate high-quality speech given text inputs. However, NTS systems may produce subpar results on texts containing unfamiliar pronunciations, context-dependent sounds, or words absent from the training dataset. To enhance regular phonetic elements while improving novel phonetic element pronunciation, we've developed a masking strategy for NTS systems. By applying a masking mask to areas of the input phonetic sequence that necessitate improvement, the system can focus on producing higher-quality speech, particularly for unfamiliar phonetic elements. To this end, we've devised an NTS framework featuring a context-aware masking module that selects masks based on context-dependent phonetic similarity. Experimental results on the CMU Arctic database and a long speech dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework, which outperforms baseline systems in predicting unfamiliar words and context-dependent phonetic elements.

We've enhanced projection predictive estimation by introducing an algorithm that projects posterior credible intervals of predictive predictions into the latent space. This modification leverages the structure of Gaussian process models, enabling more efficient computations. We've also developed a method to determine optimal projection dimensions, which balances model complexity with the accuracy of predictions. Our evaluation demonstrates that this updated approach outperforms other methods when assessing model fit and leaves other methods on par when evaluating prediction accuracy.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, which can be generated using a range of techniques including evolutionary algorithms and approximate linear programming. These malicious inputs can potentially be introduced into a DNN through a Man-in-the-Middle attack before reaching the classifier, allowing an attacker to manipulate the model's output and compromise system security. A novel attack has been devised that utilizes a malicious generative model to create malicious inputs at the time of attack, with an accompanying generative model that can be shared across multiple targets. This attack has been successfully tested on commercial VPN services and a real-world online banking system, with further investigation into the following questions in this study: the feasibility of creating malicious inputs at the time of attack, the scope of potential targets and the difficulty of detecting this type of attack.

Systematic climate change denial spreads rapidly through online platforms, despite the vast majority of scientists agreeing on its scientific facts. This study examines the characteristics of false climate change beliefs held by Twitter users in the United States, specifically those promoted by deniers and disseminated on the platform. We analyzed 20 prevalent "climate change hoax" theories found on Twitter and their associated posts, which were viewed over 1.6 billion times by over 100 million unique viewers. These theories were grouped into four categories: blame shifting, reality distortion, conspiracy theories, and denial of science. A notable phenomenon observed was that accounts owned by news organizations, politicians, and other high-profile users helped spread these false theories, often without commenting on their falsity. This suggests that online platforms are being exploited by established figures to influence public opinion on a significant issue like climate change.

A study focused on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using the CMS detector. This study analyzed a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of collisions. It differs from earlier studies which focused solely on dark matter creation accompanied by a top quark pair by also investigating cases where a top quark was present individually. Multiple criteria for selecting data categories that correspond to either a top quark or a top quark pair were developed to determine the outcomes of this study. No notable discrepancies with respect to the standard model predictions were discovered during the analysis. This data is explained within a simplified theoretical framework which includes the decay of a scalar or pseudoscalar mediator, which in turn has multiple possible masses in relation to the dark matter particle. This theoretical framework is tested across a wide range of the mediator and dark matter particle mass. This data is then compared to the expected results of a theoretical model which posits that the mediator couples equally to quarks and dark matter particles, resulting in the creation of a top quark plus missing energy signal being reduced by approximately 50%.

Given a finite category C and a representation dimension d, we define n-exdated categories as having the same representation theory as modified versions of C with a limited number of split subcategories removed. This duality matches the Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality for finite categories, extending it to n-exdated categories, which also maintains compatibility with the Morita equivalence theorem.

Building upon the concept of ranking functions, established by Flaxman, Goldstein, and Jensen in 2011, we develop a theoretical framework for modeling complex social dynamics and provide evidence of its applicability in the context of higher education. Our approach recognizes that the ultimate outcome of interest may not be directly measured and are influenced by various unobserved factors, which are often impacted by the receiver's characteristics. Additionally, the parties involved may have distinct preferences for the intervention's results. Furthermore, the instrumental variable may not consistently outperform the receiver's initial preferences as an outcome predictor. Despite these obstacles, we show that under specific conditions the ranking function method can determine the legitimate causal effects of the instrument, even in the presence of noncomparable interventions. To validate this theory, we conducted a study examining how the average salaries of graduates in different fields vary relative to one another. Utilizing data from the United States, we found evidence supporting the causal ranking effect, which confirms the existing literature on this topic. Our analysis also highlights the rationale behind utilizing the ranking function method rather than traditional causal inference techniques in this context.

A novel nuclear physics research facility is proposed, leveraging the high-energy X-ray beams generated by a state-of-the-art, high-precision J/psi storage ring. This will create an exceptionally abundant source of antineutrons, along with various hyperons and other unusual atoms, providing a vast supply of these particles. With its immense production capacity, this facility will supply a wide range of exotic atomic beams, serving as a reference point for comparisons with future antiproton factories. Its capabilities will further encompass high-precision experiments in nuclear and particle physics, as well as in quantum gravity research, astroparticle physics and materials science. In particular, the facility will offer unique opportunities to study antineutron catalyzed nucleon pair creation in dense matter, potentially revealing new insights into the symmetry energy of heavy nuclei at sub-normal densities. Additionally, it will enable the search for n-bar n-bar to p p p transitions in solid matter at various densities, as well as the test of matter with non-trivial topological properties by means of nuclear matrix elements involving valence electrons. Moreover, it will provide a vast supply of exotic atoms to study their interaction with matter, including Tauler's effect, as well as tetravalent states of antineutrons and other unusual atoms. Lastly, it will offer a vast supply of radioactive materials, serving as an essential companion to antiproton factories in nuclear physics research.

Most of the important data necessary to compute the accretion speeds in hierarchical triple systems has not been collected in a single study before. In our paper, we measure the accretion speeds in a group of systems consisting of a binary with mass ratio approximately equal to three and an outer companion, and a disc that orbits around them. We used data from the Wide Angle Shahryar survey and found 13 systems that match our search criteria, 7 of which were also included in the Far Far Away Triple Catalog.
