This outcome is derived from establishing the closeness of a specific class of controls, referred to as '(L1)-limited controls,' which satisfies the requirement of being bounded in the L1 norm. Furthermore, our analysis shows that any mild solution can be represented as the limit of a sequence of (L1)-limited controls.

Recent analyses of Galactic stellar filaments have revealed patterns suggesting these structures originated from filamentary star-forming complexes spreading across the cosmos. We re-evaluate these findings by examining the 21st Century Sky Survey's star distribution data across the Milky Way. Upon conducting our investigation, we discovered that what appear to be stellar filaments in three-dimensional depth analysis actually constitute a relatively small percentage of total celestial structures. Moreover, even though these entities exhibit seemingly linear arrangements in 2-dimensional observations, they do not maintain consistent linear patterns in 3-dimensional views. By comparing our results with established cosmic star-forming filament databases, we find that these entities lack distinct characteristics from other types of celestial objects. Based on our data, we deduce that these so-called stellar filaments are likely the result of our limited view from within the Milky Way, restricting our ability to observe star distributions in their true spatial arrangement. We speculate that these structures may appear as distinct, linear formations in other galaxies observed from afar. By acknowledging these findings, we hope to redirect attention towards a long-overlooked theory suggesting that these so-called stellar filaments are actually edge-to-face viewing of nearby galaxy stellar distribution, rather than exotic cosmic formations.

Visual item combinations, such as outfits, can be analyzed through Incompatibility Analysis (IA), which identifies unappealing or unlikely item pairings. Most existing methods are based on general pre-training techniques and ignore the intricacies of visual combinations. In response, we present VICTOR, a novel fashion-specific framework that excels at visual incompatibility identification. VICTOR's effectiveness stems from two key components: 1) a custom-made, fashion-focused language model, and 2) a feature extractor that leverages contrastive learning to preserve essential details from the item images. By integrating these modules with a Transformer-based encoder, VICTOR can effectively learn to distinguish compatible from incompatible item pairs. Through rigorous testing on existing outfits and newly created datasets, as well as comparison with four baseline methods, we demonstrate VICTOR's exceptional performance and provide actionable insights that enhance its interpretability.

Building on conventional resource theories in quantum optics, recent advancements have adapted this framework to illuminate quantum systems using a range of non-traditional resources, encompassing both classical and quantum light sources. To better capture the diversity of natural phenomena, novel conceptual and mathematical tools have been developed, allowing for a broader analysis of the underlying physics. This article serves as an introduction, outlining key ideas and methodologies that have emerged in the field.

As the number of devices contributing to a distributed machine learning model grows, the challenge of synchronizing updates can become a bottleneck. The Federated Learning framework has developed techniques to optimize communication efficiency, such as utilizing buffered aggregation and asynchronous updates. Building on this progress, this research explores the possibility of liberating models from constraint during asynchronous updates. Theoretical justifications and experimental evidence support the effectiveness of this approach.

This study explores the test function space $^\prime\mathcal{E}}_{\mathbb{R}^d}$, consisting of infinitely differentiable functions with compact support, and its relationship with the algebra of polynomial tempered distributions. We define a countable basis for $^\prime\mathcal{E}}_{\mathbb{R}^d}$ and establish the existence of a continuous dual operator mapping from $^\prime\mathcal{E}}_{\mathbb{R}^d}$ to the space of rapidly decreasing functions. Our work extends the concepts of and connections between various function spaces, incorporating the $B_G^{\lambda,\mu}$ type and the space of Markov processes, to the setting of polynomial tempered distributions.

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of additional dimensions. We've discovered that, in a five-dimensional space, the scarcity of dark energy is consistent if the scalar dark energy's slope exceeds a certain threshold. Additionally, within four-dimensional theories, the scarcity of dark energy is consistent if the slope is greater than a different, albeit related, value. We speculate that primordial black holes might constitute a significant fraction of dark matter and, in a four-dimensional space, their mass density would be sufficient to explain dark energy's observed scarcity.

A floating layer of cells that move together is known as a cell raft. Research has discovered that cell rafts composed of red blood cells exhibit periodic patterns of slow movement and rapid movement due to the closure of gaps within the raft. When gaps in the raft bridge, they creates localized pressure changes that stimulate temporary movements in the surrounding cells. Through the use of a simplified mathematical model, the behavior of these periodic patterns has been studied, and the findings have been supported by an experimental analysis of red blood cell rafts. The observed dynamics of the cell raft can be attributed to two primary factors: the reduction in surface area due to gap closure and the cell's tendency to move towards lower tensions. By manipulating these elements within the mathematical model, the various states of cell raft behavior have been replicated. Furthermore, the model has allowed for the determination of the distribution of gap sizes within the raft, and the relationship between the average gap size and the raft's density has been identified. The relationship between the average gap size and the raft's density has been determined. The presented theory offers an explanation for the observed density dependence of the cell raft's dynamics and provides a potential universal law that governs cell raft behavior.

The incorporation of strain-induced mass variations has been confirmed as a viable means of increasing hole concentrations in gallium nitride by matching the lattice structure of gallium nitride to that of zinc germanium nitride and magnesium silicon nitride. Following a review of the basic principles and strain-induced mass modification, this study examines the results of numerical simulations relating to p-type dopant activation energy and theoretical hole concentration. These findings are supplemented by an examination of strain-induced effects on fundamental properties of gallium nitride, along with experimental evidence of matching strain on hole concentration, as measured via Hall effect and photoinduced absorption measurements.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  Underwater robots struggle with data efficiency due to costly model training, poor data use, and TD target calculation, which often results in slow convergence or subpar performance.  To overcome these limitations, we've integrated a Sparse Gaussian Process that adapts during learning, allowing for data selection, TD target calculation, and policy improvement.  By using a GP-based selector, we've enhanced data utilization and eliminated the need for a dynamic model, which is often inaccurate in underwater environments.  Additionally, our method integrates the selector with a GP-based TD algorithm that calculates optimized targets from the selected data.  This approach has proven successful in various underwater navigation tasks and outperforms existing methods in several key areas, including faster convergence and more efficient policy improvements.  You can find additional details about this research in the linked paper.

We expand upon isothermic surfaces with Gaussian curvature expressions that contain meromorphic functions. New transformations are applied to these surfaces using Darboux and Calapso methods, resulting in novel isothermic surfaces.

This research explores the development of space-adaptive estimators for conditional expectation operators within the context of stationary $\alpha$-mixing processes. A nonparametric approach is introduced, consisting of a weighted, localized average of data values, conditioned on relevant sample information. Key aspects of this estimator are the selection of its support and the magnitude of its weights. Our investigation demonstrates that, under specified assumptions, this estimator precisely recovers the conditional expectation at a rate equivalent to $n^{-1/2}\cdot(\log n)^{1/2}$. Notably, the challenge posed by its nonparametric nature is highlighted by the fact that, in the absence of smoothing, many conditional expectations cannot be estimated consistently using parametric estimators. To establish consistency, our analysis relies on boundary lemmas, which provide precise bounds on probability tail weights associated with the estimator's errors. Additionally, we develop a consistent cross-validation method for determining an optimal set of weights, and investigate the behavior of this estimator within the context of its classical nonparametric counterpart.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We explore and define the $\lambda$-analogues of two specific types of $r$-Stirling numbers: ${\mathsf S}_{2,r,n}^{(1)}$ and ${\mathsf S}_{2,r,n}^{(2)}$. We derive new identities that incorporate these $\lambda$-analogues and provide a comparison with their ordinary counterparts. We also discuss potential future research avenues.

The anticipated outcomes of interest in knowledge graphs can be described as temporal link predictions. Current models, which blend static and dynamic approaches, typically struggle to achieve efficiency and scalability, hindering their use in large-scale knowledge graph challenges. This research outlines a novel, static-based temporal link prediction framework, which does not create a dynamic database and can therefore process vast knowledge graphs quickly. The proposed model, which incorporates a learnable transformer-based scoring system, can offer different levels of performance flexibility. The model's effectiveness was demonstrated on various evaluation metrics in two public datasets. Although static models are generally less effective than dynamic models, the results show that the proposed static model can hold its own against dynamic models in two public datasets. The data and code for this research are accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/juance/Static-TLP.

This note enhances and expands upon recent findings by Brown and the author, extending them to cover hereditary subcategories of row-finite graph C*-algebras, as well as a broader class of C*-algebras, in relation to a refined definition of shift equivalence.

In this research, we have examined the complex heavy quark propagator in terms of Landau levels in a quantum chromodynamics theory framework at finite magnetic fields and strong interaction conditions. By incorporating the anisotropic external magnetic field into the study, we have crystallized the heavy quark decay process and its dependency on magnetic fields, revealing crucial insights into heavy quark character displacement due to magnetic fields, which can be verified through heavy quark effective field theory and experimental studies.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about entities and their relationships. Integrating knowledge graphs, a specialized database, provides the necessary knowledge to enrich language models' capabilities. We've developed a novel approach that incorporates knowledge graph inference into these models, enabling them to utilize various logical operators and 11 possible logical expressions. Through this method, language models can derive answers even when there's a lack of explicit knowledge graph connections, as they can generate required intermediate entities through inference. We've demonstrated the efficacy of this approach by achieving top-ranked performance on Quasar, a renowned question answering dataset, with our enhanced models. Notably, our models performed over 300% better than baseline language models, solidifying the significance of knowledge graph inference in empowering these models.

Research into set cover problems has led to a significant advancement in creating high-dimensional extenders through the use of column subset selection. This involves transforming a set cover instance into a linear system, where specific column subsets can be efficiently identified to cover any given number of columns. This has resulted in the development of new high-dimensional extenders, surpassing previous ones in performance, with additional insights into achieving near-linear solutions when column subsets are available after covering initial columns. This has the potential to lead to new algorithms for set cover, particularly in scenarios with sparse matrices. This work also shows that achieving sublinear solutions in such cases requires essentially linear-time effort, assuming it is not possible to solve the group Steiner problem in sublinear time. This reveals a crucial lower bound for the set cover problem with column subsets. This lower bound is also shown to apply to high-dimensional extenders, making it a significant measure of the difficulty of set cover in such scenarios. This work also presents a simple, efficient algorithm that finds solutions of size $O(\log n)$ in scenarios with column subsets, even when the ratio of non-base columns to base columns is arbitrarily large. This implies that the dependence on $\Delta$ in previous high-dimensional extenders can be eliminated. This work is also shown to yield improved fractional solutions to set cover with constraints, surpassing previous results and the performance of the standard LP relaxation. This is achieved by recycling waste columns from previous iterations based on their distribution in the constraint matrix. This results

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error, making it a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy, particularly when it comes to multi-step tasks that require logical reasoning. Our investigation aims to address this challenge by evaluating the relationship between prompt characteristics and performance across a range of tasks, including natural language inference, logic-based tasks, and those requiring emotional understanding. Our findings suggest that model performance is boosted when prompts employ specific linguistic features, such as hypernyms, and demonstrate logical connections through words like "accordingly." Additionally, prompts that mirror written language and minimize grammatical structure seem to enhance model performance compared to their corresponding sentence-based prompts.

We assign to an Artin symbol $\sigma\mod\Delta_S$ a family of mod $\mathscr{L}$-invariants, where $\mathscr{L}$ is an irreducible automorphic representation, by leveraging the connections between Hida theory, Artin theory, and the specific $\mathscr{L}$-invariants previously introduced by Darmon-Diamond-Roberts-Vojta and made sense of broadly across various $\mathscr{L}$ scenarios. The process of connecting $\sigma$ to $\mathscr{L}$-invariants involves selecting 'intermediate' Galois stable $\mathscr{A}$-modules for a certain number field $K$ for which $\sigma$ has implications, and then mapping 'images' of its images under two distinct mappings to respectively relate $\sigma$ to modules and to $\mathscr{L}$-invariants, specifically within a critical $p$-ramified context. Notably, connections here also implicitly address non-regular weight cases where this weight is influenced by weights of certain cusp forms. Furthermore, connections here also implicitly address non-regular weight cases where this weight is influenced by weights of certain cusp forms.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms only 
react strongly to frequencies with a specific relationship to one another, 
making it hard to analyze the signals directly. Our study demonstrates that by 
training Rydberg atoms in combination with deep neural networks, it becomes possible 
to extract frequencies automatically, without needing prior knowledge. This 
breaks through a limitation of past techniques and brings us closer to applying 
these atoms in frequency resolution applications.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a massive HII region. The low surface brightness of the galaxy makes it challenging to obtain optical spectra, but a study using near-infrared spectroscopy reveals its stellar population. The analysis indicates that the galaxy consists of multiple components with diverse stellar populations. A significant portion of its mass is comprised by old, hot stars confined to a small area, suggesting a distinct outer region of the galaxy. The study also detects weak ionized gas emission in the galaxy's center, followed by a dramatic transition to a massive near-kinematical coincidence with a thick gaseous disk detected through H-alpha mapping. The fuel for the galaxy's star formation appears to reside in this stable disk, hosting the fuel for the galaxy's star formation. The findings from UGC 8839 indicate that this stable disk is a widespread phenomenon, affecting galaxies with low star formation levels. The discovery of this disk is essential to understanding how galaxies with low star formation levels are stabilized due to their massive stable disks.

For a minimally oriented quasiregular mapping that is nonconstant and comformally regular, we prove that the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set is less than or equal to one. Furthermore, if the mapping has a particular average behavior (on average, it acts like a biholomorphism) over a specific region with a particular characteristic (its boundary consists of polycircular domains), we demonstrate that the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set is less than one. Our findings build upon previous research of the second author and the first author's recent results.

Using the MODIS dataset, researchers found evidence of gravity waves in the Earth's atmosphere, primarily caused by wind and other processes. The same team, now expanded with additional members, analyzed the Mars atmosphere, examining the behavior of gravity waves from 100 to 200 km in elevation, and their results are presented in this study. The study utilized density measurements from four spacecraft: Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Odyssey, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution Nexus, and analyzed the horizontal and vertical propagation of these waves. The study found that although these waves propagate horizontally at the speed of the background wind, they can vertically bounce back due to instability, and then travel horizontally once more. The frequency of these waves could be used to determine their stability, and the study found that while most waves were stable, those observed at 123.5 Hz were not, and may have caused the instability, however more research is needed to confirm this. The study also found that while most waves propagate horizontally in the west direction, those observed at 123.5 Hz, however, are an exception, moving east instead. The study found that the phase speed of these waves is directly proportional to their frequency. The study also validated the use of the spacecraft as a tool to observe the Martian atmosphere, and observed that although the oscillations induced by the gravity waves are below the detection limit of the spacecraft's accuracy, they are still clearly visible in the data.

The LHCb and the ALICE experiment have provided precise measurements of the ALICE's J/psi production rates in Pb-Pb collisions at energies of 5.02 TeV. J/psi is produced through the nuclear break-up and cold nuclear matter interactions due to the photon-photon interaction and in collisions involving nucleon-antinucleon pairs. This textbook explanation requires validation through comparisons with data from both the LHCb and ALICE experiments. In this investigation, the ALICE's J/psi detection rates were measured in both forward and central angles during the 2015-2018 Pb-Pb data collection. In this presentation, the ALICE's recent findings on the J/psi production rates in Pb-Pb collisions are presented. The focus is on the analysis of the J/psi differential cross-section at the 5.02 TeV energy, tested against various factors including rapidity, transverse momentum, and mean transverse momentum. Additionally, the experiment examined forward J/psi production rates in Pb-Pb collisions at rapidities of -2.5 and 3.2. Mean J/psi transverse momentum was found at rapidity -2.5, while measurements at rapidity 3.2 await confirmation due to low collected data counts in this forward section. In a related study, the ALICE's experiment compared the mean pT means of J/psi and D0 mesons in Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 Te

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual guidance have led to the creation of highly realistic sounds and music, yet current methods are unacceptably inefficient, taking hours to generate a single second of audio. To overcome this limitation, we develop VDSGenerator, a cutting-edge model that combines the strengths of transformer and convolutional neural networks to produce high-quality soundscapes in a rapid manner. By integrating a visual feature extractor with a sound-specific token-based generator, VDSGenerator achieves exceptional both in terms of accuracy and speed, outperforming leading competitors while generating sound waves up to 50 times faster.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) address the limitation of traditional feedforward networks by capturing temporal relationships in sequential data, enabling them to model dynamic behaviors in various contexts, such as natural language processing, stock market analysis, and audio recognition. This paper delves into RNN's fundamental principles and applies them to sequential prediction tasks.

Finding a balance between economic well-being and public health during a pandemic pandemic is a difficult task. To achieve this, we must determine the optimal timing and extent of various measures such as lockdowns, vaccination campaigns, and border closures. By employing an advanced mathematical model, we developed a comprehensive framework for analyzing policy interventions in a pandemic model featuring two distinct disease phases and an interconnected multi-regional structure. The results show that measures such as lockdowns, vaccination campaigns, and border closures can be represented by a single unified formula that applies equally to different scenarios. The optimal policy timing is dependent on specific circumstances but is generally influenced by the pandemic's transmissibility, mortality rates, and other key factors. The implemented policies have a proportional impact on disease severity and recovery times. For a two-phase pandemic, the optimal timing is influenced by the relative durations of different phases, as well as the gap between the peak deaths under non-intervention and the peak infections under the best possible outcomes. Furthermore, our model allows for the analysis of policy effects at both the regional and global levels, thus providing actionable insights for policymakers aimed at mitigating the economic and health impacts of a pandemic.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is facilitated by various software tools that manage large datasets, enable efficient processing, and ensure data quality. These software tools, referred to as data debugging tools, cater to developers and data scientists who require advanced data analytics capabilities to debug their code, data, and computations. We propose a unified framework for data debugging that encompasses existing approaches and introduces a novel concept, Shapley Significance, to identify crucial data segments affecting model outcomes. This is accomplished through a systematic evaluation of various debugging techniques and machine learning pipelines that highlight the importance of data segmentation and demonstrate Shapley Significance to be a effective and efficient debugging strategy.

This work explores various combinations of the aforementioned fields by
enumerating graphical models, analyzing tensor networks, and studying loop models.
Specifically, we delve into the asymptotic enumeration of random simple graphs,
random ratio matrices, and random ratio loops. To achieve this, we develop
mathematical frameworks that incorporate a new approach to degree-based
generating functions and precise estimates for the critical probability distribution
in zero-temperature quantum criticality. These models hold crucial significance as
they accurately represent the thermodynamic properties of quantum systems. Building
on established ideas, including past work and research on ratio schemes, our
approach provides significant insights into the underlying probability distributions.

This study provides the first observation of high pressure-induced trimerization and the associated crossover of the anomalous Hall effect in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn. At low pressure, the material exhibits a 120-degree ordering with a moderate anomalous Hall effect, but at higher pressures, it transitions into an effective ferromagnetic state with significantly enhanced anomalous Hall effect. This transition is monitored through in-situ synchrotron x-ray diffraction and is accompanied by increased long-range order and trimerization that surpasses that at low pressure, along with pressure-dependent magnetic and electrical measurements.

The rapidly evolving business landscape compels organizations to stay abreast of emerging trends and competitor activity to maintain market supremacy. To achieve this, companies need to accurately extract key information from various sources, such as news articles, to assess competitors, industry developments, and their own performance. This document surveys the rising influence of Deep Neural Networks within the realm of Information Extraction in business contexts since 2014. Several recent studies have employed DNN-based techniques to extract meaningful relationships between organizational entities. This review synthesizes the most current research in this area, covering topics such as sentence-level semantic analysis, relation categorization, domain-specific language understanding, and data formatting for machine learning. By consolidating existing knowledge and identifying areas for further investigation, this document serves as an introduction and reference for newcomers to the field, bridging the gap between broadly available surveys on related topics and the growing number of research papers focused on business-specific information extraction applications.

This article discusses a variation of the Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem, introducing a key aspect - the existence of at least one eigenvalue - via a well-established topological approach. We then build on this framework by incorporating additional conditions, such as the allowance of measure, to expand upon our initial findings.

We are given a complete hypergraph where the large edges have been removed, 
and we want to use the remaining vertices and remaining edges to estimate the 
original structure. This is known as the guided hypergraph reconstruction problem, 
and we can use a method called maximum likelihood estimation to solve it. We've 
developed a statistical model to analyze this problem and have found that 
as the number of vertices grows, the estimated solution gets closer to the 
original structure under certain conditions. Our experiments confirm the 
findings and provide further insight into this problem.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data,
specifically X-Rays and CT scans. Current natural language processing techniques for
medical report understanding have been hindered by the lack of high-quality annotated
data, particularly due to the difficulties and expenses associated with manually
labeling such data. We have developed an innovative approach to create detailed
annotations for chest X-Ray images, enabling us to train effective models for
extracting relevant data from radiology reports. Our data annotation process
automatically generates labels for findings, conditions, treatments, and other
important report elements, using synthetic labels derived from from CT scan
projections. This method allows us to train a segment proposal network (SPN) that
accurately identifies and extracts relevant information from the images. Our
training data comprises 28,000 images with manually written findings and 200,
000 sentences describing related medical information. We have achieved notable
results, with our SPN model accurately pinpointing relevant regions in images
alongside their corresponding labels in 76.7% of cases. Our data can be accessed at
https://www.unicarneurobic.github.io/ CXR-Labels/.

Tight contact structures have become increasingly prominent due to their inherent rigidity. Given a tight contact 3-manifold, defining the Thurston norm is achievable and it possesses key properties, such as non-negativity and circular inequality. The Euler characteristic can be determined for any positive norm value. The set of possible Euler characteristic values for a fixed positive norm value can be any integer 0 to infinity, including jumps and discontinuities. The presence of singularities complicates things as it sometimes results in reduced characteristic values. The relationship between the Euler characteristic and the norm is not a linear or polynomial function.

Three-dimensional lattice hydrodynamics models, inspired by hydrodynamic models of quantum systems, have suggested enhanced photon diffusion and flow could lead to entropic losses in directionally emitting microcavity lasers. However, the underlying hydrodynamic framework's connection to actual quantum systems has been called into question. Instead, we investigated this phenomenon using a quantum point charge model that assumes charges obey non-relativistic quantum mechanics. By establishing a relationship between entropy and radial and tangential photon velocity components, we found that entropic losses can occur due to photon collisions generating heat within the cavity. Additionally, we discovered that directionally emitting microcavity lasers are more prone to entropic losses than randomly emitting ones. Notably, our findings confirm that entropic losses can arise from global phenomena caused by individual charges' emissions.

We've developed a model to study the stability of cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, and our findings support three key conclusions. Firstly, in the long term, the value of cryptocurrencies is likely to be consistent, albeit fluctuating in the short term. This instability in the short term can be attributed to the volatile nature of investors' confidence levels in the currency. In contrast, the value of cryptocurrencies in the long term is relatively stable due to the inherent characteristics of the underlying blockchain technology, which ensures security and durability. Secondly, the price of cryptocurrencies tends to converge towards their long-term value over time, and the rate of convergence is influenced by the rate at which investors' confidence levels in the currency are adjusted. In other words, the speed at which the price of cryptocurrencies reaches its stable value is relatively high compared to other types of assets. Thirdly, the current price of cryptocurrencies is likely to be lower than its stable value, which in turn indicates the potential for further growth in the near future.

Solving the nonlinear Schrödinger equation and integrating the molecular dynamics equation were pivotal in addressing the laminar flow regime of the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation, a problem initially posed by Quastel and Walker. By applying similar methods to a broader nonlinear Schrödinger equation, we derived a "weak noise" regime for KPZ, featuring a $2/3$ exponent, thereby validating the existing, numerically-derived results and predicting a $-1/2$ correction term.

We discuss how magnetic field fluctuations measured by the Magnetospheric MultiScale (MMS) spacecraft at similar times can provide crucial information about the scale and orientation of compressive plasma waves. When spaced at a distance of approximately 20 code lengths, or about 110 meters, the fluctuations in spacecraft potential show significant differences under solar wind plasma conditions that are either aligned or perpendicular to each other. This distinction occurs because the potential fluctuations can represent the electric field of the wave when the electric and magnetic fields are parallel, but remain static and unrelated when they are perpendicular. Measurements of the perpendicular configuration reveal fluctuations with scales and orientations varying due to solar wind plasma interfaces. In contrast, the parallel configuration shows fluctuations that appear to be a shared property of solar wind plasma interfaces. These findings are corroborated by computer simulations that model the electron responses to these interfaces in the solar wind, confirming that the perpendicular configuration allows electric and magnetic fields to decouple and that parallel configurations show shared properties among multiple interfaces.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts. This advancement may expand access to attosecond science to a broader user community, bringing it within reach of existing and future facilities such as the FLASH and LCLS.

A mathematical model of a stratified flow is developed to estimate the development of smooth shear layers using direct perturbation techniques based on physical optics approximation. This model assumes a varying density profile across a smooth shear layer, which can be categorized into three types: linear, logistic, and exponential variations. By applying the WKB approximation and incorporating second-order corrections to account for focal effects, a general framework is formulated to estimate key hydrodynamic parameters, such as viscous dissipation, Froude and Reynolds numbers, and critical layer location. These parameters are calculated by applying the Adomian series solution to the modified Korteweg-de Vries equation, which describes the behavior of long-wavelength internal waves. A detailed analysis is performed to evaluate the accuracy of third-order estimates for various types of density profiles and a parameter study is conducted to investigate how changes to key model parameters affect the estimated outcomes.

Building upon previous research that applied simulated annealing to quantify gerrymandering, we propose an enhanced algorithm. Despite the original method's effectiveness in detecting extreme cases, it falls short in accurately estimating the true level of gerrymandering in a given district. Our improved protocol not only runs in near-linear time, but it also generates a confidence interval for its estimates. Furthermore, we devised a series of tests to ensure the reliability of our approach.

A novel defect identification approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, to accurately locate defects on fabric edges. Since defects typically exhibit irregular movement across the edge, this descriptor leverages this behavior to effectively pinpoint the region of interest. Following defect detection, a low-rank decomposition technique is applied to the defect area to achieve high-quality defect images, where the sum of two orthogonal projections closely approximates the original image, and thus highlighting the remaining features. This methodology demonstrates superior results compared to existing techniques.

To learn visual guidelines from limited annotated data, research has shown that incorporating prior knowledge into reinforcement learning is beneficial. The main drawback of existing approaches lies in their reliance on uncertain shape priors. In our research, we introduce a new method to derive visual guidelines by leveraging statistical characteristics of object shapes. The proposed framework utilizes information-theoretic regularization terms in both reinforcement learning and neural networks to enhance the guidelines' clarity and stability. The experimental outcomes confirm that our approach can effectively learn visual guidelines for novel scenarios.

A large-scale black hole (BSH) at the center of a cluster galaxy is assumed to have caused the burst's energy output. We use the property that BSHs emit energy over an approximately $10^7$ year cycle to set an upper limit on mass lost due to Bondi accretion. We derive that the average mass added to the BSH is no more than $10^{59}$ grams per year, or $3.2 \times 10^{-6} M_\odot$ per year, assuming the BSH has a $10^9 M_\odot$ mass and an average gas density that varies as $r^{-2}$, where $r$ is the distance from the BSH. This limit on Bondi accretion helps explain the relatively low energy output of central BSHs in galaxy clusters by preventing them from accumulating enough mass and rapidly growing their accretion rates needed to produce the observed radio data. It also helps resolve the discrepancy between observations of radio data and predictions of energy output based on the BSH's potential.

We examine the formation of the primary elements such as hydrogen, helium, and heavier nutrients in the core of early star clusters using a cosmological and realistic model. It's discovered that in the context of early universe star clusters formed through collapse, the supply of these primary elements is significantly lower than in clusters formed through mergers. Furthermore, when we simulate the collapse of these clusters, it's found that the cluster with lower primary element abundance experiences more extreme collapse, leading to the formation of a black hole. In contrast, the cluster with higher primary element abundance avoids total collapse, giving rise to a black hole with lower mass. Using a cosmological and realistic model, we investigate the gravitational waves emitted by these low-mass and high-mass black holes formed from early star cluster collapses, with a focus on their potential detectability by future gravitational wave observatories. It's discovered that although early star cluster collapses produce fewer low-mass black holes, their gravitational waves can be more easily detected due to higher emission rates, largely offsetting this disadvantage. Additionally, early star cluster collapses remain a dominant source of low-mass gravitational wave production out to z=2, with their high-mass black hole signals remaining detectable in future gravitational wave observatories until z=8.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. There's also a rising risk of significant fires that canOrigin from faulty smart equipment. We're proposing a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents in real-time within a power distribution network. This approach leverages an automated machine learning framework to create a universal incident detection model, capable of recognizing anomalies in a power flow vector, whether or not a specific pattern has been previously identified. We'll provide detailed examples of this method using actual data from a power distribution network.

Our study focuses on examining the radiative and electromagnetic decays of the $X(3872)\pi\gamma$ and involve determining the X(3872) form factor. To achieve this, we employed two methods: 

  The first used a Lagrangian description to calculate the form factor, accounting for the X(3872) composition under quark and resonance matter. 
  The second method involved a phenomenological approach using the X(3872) decay to J/psi pi pi, and applicable corrections for radiative decay to J/psi pi gamma. 

Our findings from the two methods show notable discrepancies in the X(3872) form factor, particularly evident at lower Q^2 values. 
The differences between the two approaches can be attributed to potential issues in the X(3872) composition, identified in our investigations. 
The X(3872) is likely a tetraquark or an excited hadronic state, and our results are comparable to both scenarios. 
The X(3872) width to radiation and pi pi radiation decays were also derived and are inclusive of non-resonant contributions. 
The X(3872) width to radiation decay lies within experimental limits, and our results for the pi pi radiation decay are consistent with current data. 
Our study offers new areas for experimental investigation and fresh perspectives on the X(3872) composition.

We provide a comprehensive description of smooth quadrics within the context of bounded symmetric domains, offering categorical representations of symplectic and arithmetic triads in the process. This description enables the classification of quadrics up to categorial equivalence, allowing us to derive insights into their geometric and arithmetic characteristics in the course of proof.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 500 actions per second, largely due to the comprehensive AI systems that drive them.
In contrast, our proposed challenge, TextWorldExpress, offers a highly optimized set of games with improved processing speeds of over one million actions per second.
To achieve this boost, we employed several strategic techniques including the integration of static levels, forward thinking algorithms, and predictive techniques that look ahead to upcoming levels and player objectives.
Furthermore, our evaluation revealed that the advanced agent competing in TextWorldExpress outperforms current benchmarks by roughly 50% across a range of challenging tasks and processes text inputs at an astonishing 3200 words per second.

The mathematical framework for studying topological insulators with defects, particularly symmetry-breaking and Anderson insulating defects, is thoroughly examined in this paper. Deformations of topological insulators are also investigated, focusing on the continuous variations of the spectral gap within various norms. This analysis draws on recent research [arXiv:2101.01367] and provides a comprehensive overview with key outcomes summarized in a table.

Consider a continuous function, f, defined on a planar sector, D, where the sector's opening angle is less than 2p. Assume f is p-harmonic within this domain. We show that if f is bounded above on D, then the local averages of f converge to its sup value as D's radius tends to infinity. This result generalizes a theorem initially proven by Jannsen and Pohlke, which estimated the local averages of a harmonic function in a planar sector. Our theorem also applies to subharmonic and superharmonic functions as well.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between weather patterns, wave heights, and coastal erosion is examined. Wave heights derived from buoy data and coastal erosion data collected at North Stradbroke Island, Australia, are analyzed to investigate the nature of their extreme relationships. A parameter estimation method is employed to examine the model's properties. The results suggest that there is a strong connection between certain types of weather, wave heights, and coastal erosion. This investigation aims to facilitate the development of a multivariate spatial model for extreme weather and wave conditions.

For a non-singular projective algebraic variety V over a number field K, we investigate the finiteness of rational maps from V to geometrically connected, non-variety spaces over K. Despite the absence of an intrinsic definition for non-singular varieties over fields other than algebraicely closed ones, our proof follows the approach of Ulmer's work on finiteness of non-constant maps over Dedekind domains.

A significant challenge in using robots effectively in everyday environments lies in navigating through unknown spaces. Human-like robots can learn from observing people in real-world situations, but their planning algorithms struggle with discrepancies between humans and robots. To bridge this gap, we develop a new method to map human manipulability tasks onto robot tasks, taking into account that task parameters exist within specific, constrained areas. Using this approach, researchers can easily transfer tasks between humans and robots, without needing to recalculate task parameters. Instead, we employ a localized, precise registration technique that considers the specific geometry and movement patterns of each task. With this method, the registration process is sped up and the results are more accurate, even in situations with partial occlusions. We test the effectiveness of our approach by demonstrating that it allows low-dimensional planners to successfully solve high-dimensional tasks.

In a study of Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ process at the LHC, we examine the potential of using the matrix element method to enhance signal detection beyond current selection methods. By comparing traditional event selection techniques with the matrix element method, we evaluate their efficiency in recovering signal events that have been mistakenly classified as background using a likelihood-based approach. Additionally, we investigate the effectiveness of these methods in reducing background contamination by creating discriminant variables.

A novel method is introduced for training 3D object pose estimation models, leveraging the widespread presence of turntables in indoor settings. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on controlled, manufactured environments, this method employs accidental turntables - everyday locations with rotating objects. These turntables are discovered using only uncurated image data. The proposed method is particularly significant due to the growing interest in CLIP, a powerful large-language-model-based image embeddings tool. Our method's key component is TurntableClip, a large dataset of 3D object pose annotations derived from Accidental Turntables - everyday locations with rotating objects. The dataset is created by combining the strengths of two existing sources: Thingi360 - a repository of 3D printing components, and the Clipmap portion of CLIP. It includes over 135k accurately labeled 2D images and 13k associated 3D poses. The method is evaluated using standard metrics on two popular datasets - PASCAL 3D+ and LINEMOD - and compared to previous approaches. Our results show substantial improvements in prediction accuracy for both semi-synthetic and fully synthetic object categories.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread through platforms like Twitter necessitates manual review by platform moderators to decide on removal or retention. This decision requires the ability to distinguish accepted factual information from rejected misinformation. In this research, we employ neural networks to predict the review team's decision regarding tweets promoting anti-vaccination misinformation. Our findings demonstrate that neural networks can accurately predict the review team's choice, showcasing the influence of misinformation on users' beliefs. Our data analysis uncovered that approximately 41% of anti-vaccination tweets have been classified as misinformation, highlighting the difficulty of neural networks in distinguishing accepted posts (identified as 'not misinformation') from rejected ones (labeled as'misinformation'). Our model's robustness was further established by assessing the consistency of labels across different sources.

Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving coherent control of attosecond pulse generation. Nevertheless, the typical incoherent plasma-based X-ray source flavor poses a significant challenge to attosecond science. This study breaks through this obstacle by leveraging a novel strong-field coherent source, which produces controlled few-femtosecond pulses containing isolated attosecond events. Through computations and experimental verification, our research demonstrates that a coherent source based on relativistic intense few-cycle laser pulses can produce single attosecond pulses, along with controlling pulse splitting. This breakthrough enables accurate measurement and regulation of isolated attosecond pulses, paving the way for the measurement of electronic dynamics in molecules and solids.

Eclipse predictions for binary and multiple star systems rely on precise data for their orbital and relative positions. To obtain these predictions, researchers have developed automatic transformations to convert data between different reference frames. However, current algorithms are not sufficiently accurate for systems involving far-off dim objects and bright background stars. To address this issue, we have created a new algorithm that automatically converts eclipse data into a standardized frame. To test its effectiveness, we applied it to 54 systems from the Algol eclipse data catalog and achieved a 75% success rate with a 2-3 second computation time per system. Our technique has particular significance for systems similar to that of Gamma Aquilae, where a new companion candidate has been recently identified.

This paper investigates the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation in a particular high-dimensional space, specifically when there's a non-compact boundary or a limited boundary within a 5 or higher dimensional space. We discover that in these scenarios, particularly when there's a bounded obstacle, solutions which have a high initial energy will eventually enter a state of infinite energy, occurring within a finite time frame, provided the total mass from the initial condition is below a specific threshold. This research builds upon previous work by Holmer and Roudenko, extending it to scenarios involving a bounded space, accounting for a variable nonlinearity of Schrödinger equations of type $-\Delta u + V_0u = F(u)$ where $F$ is a polynomial or power-law function that may include terms like $\frac{-u^{\frac{9}{2}(p+1)}}{|x|^5^{(p+1)}}$ where $p$ is an integer value of $-1$ or higher.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency and accuracy are required for this approach. To address these requirements, enhancing the approximation architecture and learning algorithm of physics-informed neural networks is essential. This research introduces a new adaptive node creation technique to enhance the approximation architecture of physics-informed neural networks. This method creates new nodes within the discrete approximation framework by analyzing the residual errors of existing nodes, incorporating a weighting factor that balances short- and long-term error reduction. This adaptive node creation method can be applied to any discrete approximation framework, including polynomial and neural network-based methods. Our study evaluates the performance of this algorithm using the heat and advection-diffusion equations, and we also investigate its ability to mitigate the effects of overfitting. Our results show that this new algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, particularly on problems with limited data.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of a multi-domain ferroelectric FET by considering both electrostatic and mechanical responses during the device's operation. By incorporating a novel mechanism known as adverse capacitance, which arises from the negative charge associated with domain wall instability, the model effectively captures the device's transient dynamics, particularly at the turn-on voltage, thereby eliminating the need for prior knowledge of charging times. Furthermore, the adverse capacitance is responsible for a significant (100%) overestimation of the ferroelectric gate's effective thickness, a critical consideration that needs to be taken into account in further ferroelectric technology advancements.

A significant portion of software projects' vulnerabilities can be attributed to dependencies within Cargo ecosystems. Conducting an in-depth examination of Cargo projects requires a comprehensive dataset in the form of a knowledge graph that captures dependency relationships. This paper outlines a two-part approach for constructing this graph: Firstly, Cargo projects along with their versioned dependencies are gathered and mapped onto a graph. Secondly, a measure of vulnerability severity is applied to nodes and directed edges, allowing for the modeling of vulnerability propagation through the graph. An experimental evaluation of this approach highlights its potential benefits and limitations. The proposed method enables the analysis of vulnerability spread across projects in the Cargo ecosystems and sheds light on best practices for minimizing vulnerability impact. An interactive visual representation of the graph can be accessed via this link: https://nus-sec-guru.github.io/Cargo-Dependency-Graph/.

For a class of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations with leap noise, we demonstrate that the solution has multiple irregularity levels and prove a key result: the filtered processes of these solutions remain irreducible at various levels of regularization. This result has important implications: first, it indicates that changing the parameters of the equation's coefficients cannot simplify the behavior of the solution; second, it implies that the truncated processes of the filtered equations cannot be factored into lower-level components; third, it has implications for the relative regularity of joint variables of the filtered equations, which is essential for understanding the behavior of the equations and developing tools for analyzing the equations' properties.

Let $G$ be a finite nilpotent group, and let $\mathcal{P}(G)$ be the power graph of $G$ defined by making the order relationship correspond to elements generated by others. We show that if $G$ is not isomorphic to a direct product of a torus and a cyclic group, then the minimum order of vertices in $\mathcal{P}(G)$ is $p^2$ for some prime $p$, resolving a previous question. Moreover, we give a description of vertices at order $p^2$ and establish that if $G$ has a prime index subgroup, then the minimum order of vertices in $\mathcal{P}(G)$ is a square greater than $p$. We also extend the definition of power graphs to groups that are not nilpotent but satisfy a certain condition, and investigate these groups known as $2$-nilpotent groups, defining a power graph as previously described by making the order relationship correspond to elements generated by others. We show that if the minimum order of vertices in $\mathcal{P}(G)$ is $p$, then $G$ has a subgroup of index $p$ contained in a nilpotent group, and we classify the resulting power graphs for groups of order $p^3$.

The Large Hadron Collider, with its cutting-edge research in particle physics, drives the development of the Small Hybrid for Intensity Detection, SHiPD. This innovative project aims to create the most advanced particle detector ever built, with a historical connection to the Fast Field-Cycle Cosmology Detector, FFCD, which was a hybrid of a hybrid detector. The SHiPD will serve two primary purposes: first, it will be used as a high-intensity beam detector at the LHC's proton beam dump target, and second, it will be employed in cosmic ray research to study the properties of antimatter using cosmic rays. With its groundbreaking features, the SHiPD will play a pivotal role in both LHC and cosmic ray research, offering unparalleled opportunities to advance our understanding of particle physics and cosmology.

Direction Convolutional Networks, a variant of Convolutional Networks, use anisotropic filters that are sensitive to image direction, expanding the representation capacity of conventional convolutional layers. By introducing a novel coordinate system, these networks can apply unique anisotropic filters in multiple orientations, effectively increasing the number of trainable parameters. Experiments have demonstrated the superior performance of DCNs over traditional convolutional networks on various image recognition tasks.

This study seeks to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of 3D object classification tasks handled through point cloud data analysis. Key contributions of this research involve conducting a comprehensive review of the current state-of-the-art models, designing a high-performance model with accurate prediction capabilities, and proposing an optimization technique to significantly reduce model complexity and processing time. A comprehensive evaluation of the models is also provided to validate their effectiveness across various scenarios.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning across different datasets. Our method incorporates a key feature - the trigger, which represents the trigger's semantic description through various image representations, thus ensuring the trigger's relevance to the targeted model, regardless of the input image. Furthermore, the trigger's semantic description is analyzed by a language model to calculate its similarity to the targeted model's activation, using the contrastive loss to ensure the trigger's uniqueness. Our experiment results in 94% accuracy on host models, with a significantly reduced spatial complexity and elevated semantic complexity compared to existing Trojan attacks. Our attack demonstrates the vulnerability of models that rely heavily on visual data, as demonstrated on ImageNet and CIFAR10 using the ResNet50 and VGG16 models.

We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will enable low-resolution observations with a 2.83 arcsecond spacing along the slit. Our current progress includes finished optics, a mask assembler, and software tools to optimize mask placement; we're now constructing the mask assembler and planning for its integration with IMACS.

In this paper, we explore the progress of the Trojan Horse Method and reveal that it has the capability to accurately measure small astrophysical $S$-factors with high precision, especially for thin targets. We update the calculation of the $S(\epsilon)=2\sigma_g B_{\rm grav} f(\epsilon)\langle\sigma v\rangle$ expression and incorporate the latest developments in the THM, highlighting its potential to measure $S$-factors with a 1% or less margin of error for this particular reaction. We outline the steps to achieve this level of precision and demonstrate the effectiveness of combining experimental and theoretical analysis to determine the reaction rate, an approach that can be applied to a broad range of other fusion reactions.

A key objective in astrophysics is to utilize star-to-exoplanet sampling to enhance our comprehension of planetary interior construction. We investigated the elemental makeup of 5 dim stars, extracted data on their basic characteristics, and applied benchmark models to 2 terrestrial planets to gain insights into their interior structures. Our findings are summarized as follows. \textit{The Bright Dim Stars}. We gathered spectroscopic information on bright dim stars with known terrestrial planets, and through standard analysis, we identified typical patterns of dimness and planetary interior models. \textit{Terrestrial Planets in the TRAPPIST-1 System}. We carried out a thorough investigation of the 7 Earth-mass planets in the TRAPPIST-1 system by applying benchmark models to each planet. We discovered that only 3 of the 7 planets have distinct or somewhat distinct dimness patterns. However, all 7 planets have compatible elemental compositions with the atmosphere of TRAPPIST-1 e being typical. \textit{Future Prospects}. Our future research will involve a more in-depth examination of the 7 planets in the TRAPPIST-1 system as well as other targets. We intend to utilize a comprehensive approach to better understand dimness and planetary interior construction.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization using channel state information (CSI), as they can effectively capture the complex relationships between CSI and location. Nevertheless, the reliability of CSI-based localization is still a concern due to the fragility of CSI to various channel disturbances. Research has revealed that incorporating location information into the model can help the network learn relevant features and enhance location prediction. Nonetheless, current studies assume that the input CSI is complete, which may not always be the case in real-world scenarios due to channel fluctuations. To address this, this paper proposes a novel attention-assisted CSI-based localization framework that can effectively learn location features from incomplete CSI. To protect the network from external channel disturbances, this framework utilizes a robust CSI generator to create a stable base CSI, then extracts location-related features from the attention-weighted cumulative sum of CSI. Experimental results demonstrate that the framework can achieve reliable localization even with severely distorted CSI.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking various systems to the categorical structure of topological categories. The study focuses on S5, K, and B logic, interpreting the logical operators in relation to categorical mappings that represent the modal context. A key aspect is the categorification of the well-known Kripke models, translating the pre-order structure into a topological category with an ordered monoidal structure. The derivation of logical laws for these systems is an essential outcome of this approach.

A graph is considered edge-colorable if a coloring can be applied where no two adjacent edges have the same color. The minimum number of colors required for this edge-coloring is denoted as χ′(G), with χ′(G) ≥ χ(G)/2, where χ(G) is the minimum number of colors needed for a vertex coloring of G. In 1961, Erdos proposed the conjecture that χ′(G) = χ(G). This theory has been supported by numerous supported findings. A theory supported by Hermon in 2019 suggested that the upper limit for edges in a graph with the maximum number of edges not requiring five colors and five as the minimum number of colors required for an edge coloring is 423. In the case of bipartite graphs, theory supported by Hermon in 2019 suggested that the upper limit for edges in a graph with the maximum number of edges not requiring three colors and three as the minimum number of colors required for an edge coloring is 421. A theory that the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph with the minimum number of edges required for an edge coloring is one edge, and three as the minimum number of colors required for an edge coloring is 421. A theory that the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph with the minimum number of edges required for an edge coloring is one edge, and three as the minimum number of colors required for an edge coloring is 421 was proven wrong

This paper explores the minimal eigenvalue among all functions defined on the Hamming graphs, given a set of coefficients that define a quadratic form on these graphs. This quadratic form is expressed as the sum of weighted pairwise differences between vertices in the graphs. By taking a standard basis of vectors as the basis for our quadratic form, we find the minimum eigenvalue can be represented as the minimum of sum of squared differences on the grid $\mathbb{Z}_q^d$ or, equivalently, the minimum of sum of squared distances in the cube $\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^d$ for any nonnegative integers $d$ and $q$. This result generalizes a recent finding by Harar and Saito regarding the eigenvalues of functions on the Hamming graphs.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but previous versions had a standalone interface that only allowed data viewing, with model editing requiring the use of a text editor. To address this limitation, a new web-based client-server system, ShinyCOPASI, has been developed to provide an interactive interface for users to explore, analyze, and modify COPASI models. ShinyCOPASI offers a range of features, including interactive visualizations, predictive model capabilities, sensitivity and uncertainty analysis, and a model editor with real-time validation, among others. To use ShinyCOPASI, users need to upload their models and upload any additional data required for analysis to a server, with the interactive interface then displaying the results of comprehensive simulations and allowing users to explore the consequences of changes in model parameters, differential equation systems, and network topology.

The significant advancements in machine learning have led to its adoption as a core component in scientific research and operations. However, the conventional focus on model performance measurement does not address the unique challenges posed by uncertain outcomes in scientific ML. To bridge this gap, we conducted a comprehensive review of existing literature on quantitative metrics for evaluating model uncertainty and developed new metrics as well as novel comparisons with existing ones. The development of novel metrics serves two purposes: initially, we created uncertainty measurement methods that align with established metrics for categorizing model performance. Secondly, we proposed specific, tailored metrics for binary and multi-class classification problems in addition to regression scenarios. The proposed metrics were then precisely defined and demonstrated to be viable alternatives to current evaluation methods. The aim is to facilitate informed model selection and tailored design for scarce data scenarios in scientific ML, thus enhancing the accuracy and reliability of predictions in such contexts.

We investigate the von Neumann algebra resulting from category functions on a compact quantum group, denoted as $C_0(\mathcal{G})$ with $\mathcal{G}$ being rich in structure. The study reveals that for a vast majority of finite quantum groups, the resulting algebra is isomorphic to the minimal quantum group's $C^*$-algebra, while we also identify specific examples where the result deviates from this pattern. Additionally, our research yields a comprehensive understanding of the Borel space connected to $C_0(\mathcal{G})$, which in turn allows us to determine the topological richness of the quantum group $C_0(\mathcal{G})$ based on the existence of certain unitary representations.

In this research, we develop a computational method for solving Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) that leverages the benefits of the Generalized Minimum Error Recovery Algorithm (GMRES) and the Krylov approximation technique to accelerate convergence, particularly for large-scale infinite-horizon problems with block-diagonal structures. To further improve efficiency, we introduce a novel variant of GMRES that incorporates a degree of uncertainty, refining previous approaches and enabling simultaneous computation of multiple eigenvalues. This results in a more practical solution for large-scale finite-horizon problems and a more accurate approximation for eigenvalue problems, enhancing both theoretical and numerical performance. Numerical case studies showcase the superiority of our approach over existing methods.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We study the sequence of edge ideals given by $I^{(n)}(\mathcal{D})$. It's proven that for a weighted directed tree, $I^{(n)}(\mathcal{D})$ is generated by quadratic edges for a sufficient number of $n$. Moreover, based on this result, we derive similar findings for linear edge ideals of directed paths. To extend this, we investigate the symbolic and typical powers of edge ideals of weighted directed cycles. Our conclusions are verified using various examples and counter-examples.

This research focuses on solving an inverse problem for complex computer simulations that generate time series data. By modeling this process, scientists can identify underlying factors that explain observed data, presenting these factors in a simplified summary. However, the computational simulation is subject to significant uncertainty due to various factors such as incomplete knowledge, limited resources, and inaccurate assumptions, all of which hinder accurate results. In many cases, the simulation is influenced by various scenarios represented by multiple contour curves, each associated with a specific set of input parameters, making total order estimation impractical due to computational constraints. In such scenarios, our proposed method, leveraging the advantages of multiple contour estimation, selects relevant parameters to generate simulated data, which is then compared with actual observations to produce a precise summary of relevant factors. Utilizing advanced Monte Carlo simulations and real-world data on COVID-19 spread and air quality in New York City, we demonstrate the efficacy and rapid run-time of our proposed approach, enabling it to process millions of parameter sets per hour.

In robust machine learning, we're addressing potential attacks on future data.
A strong model must perform well on most datasets similar to the original one.
Our focus is on how much a dataset can change (its "density"] before a model's guarantees fall apart.
We're investigating whether individual properties of datasets influence how robust the models are.
To approach this, we're using specific density measures that can be easily understood and calculated.
Then, for each of these measures, we're establishing specific conditions under which local inquiries can effectively ensure robustness.
For instance, when datasets are dense enough around the original one, local inquiries suffice to achieve robustness.
However, when datasets become more chaotic and individual properties are less consistent, other mechanisms are required to reach robustness.
Ultimately, local inquiries provide valuable additional tools for achieving robustness but are substitutable if the density is low.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with isolated photons in PbPb collisions have been measured. Analyses of charged-hadron pair distributions and neutral hadron fractions allow for observations of changes in jet fragmentation due to interactions with the quark-gluon plasma. Results from PbPb collisions show decreases in long-range hadron production and increased neutral hadron formation at the end of jet fragmentation, indicating alterations to jet fragmentation caused by the quark-gluon plasma.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of evaluating related multiple zeta values in fractional or "colored" forms. In light of this, we have developed new approaches to computing specific types of such values. Specifically, we have derived explicit formulas for certain series of the form \sum_{m_n \geq 1,..., m_k <... < m_0 = 0} m_0^a m_1... m_k^b m_n <... m_1 m_2 m_3 = 0, where the summation indices m_0,..., m_k are alternately colored as being "black" or "white", with k an even integer. We have provided multiple zeta function and related hypergeometric series counterparts to these results, with their respective Henle-Bertin-Merciante type formulas serving as fundamental building blocks for our work. In particular, we have established that the colored fundamental series of the form \sum_{m_n \geq 1,..., m_k <... < m_0 = 0} m_0^a m_1... m_k^b m_n <... m_1 m_2 m_3 = 0 can be expressed as colored colander variants of related multiple zeta functions. In a related finding, we have identified a distinct class of colored multiple zeta functions for which we have determined the associated colored colander values. In computing these

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, failed to confirm the photometric data obtained by Meisner et al, indicating an extremely bright sub-stellar object was mistakenly identified. The initial findings suggested the presence of a L7 or M2 dwarf based on a low flux comparison with standard reference sources. The main discrepancy lies in the initial report's 20.5 magnitud difference between WISE and 2MASS photometry, versus the expected 6-7 magnitud difference for a typical L or M dwarf. Further investigation is needed to determine whether the anomaly results from unusual photometric data or an unusual object requiring re-evaluation of the initial findings.

The subatomic particles created in Xe-Xe nucleus collisions at the LHC's CERN research facility are examined through a comprehensive analysis of the ALICE detector data and Monte Carlo simulations. This study models the formation and tracking of these particles as they are produced in the events. A detailed computation of the relative probabilities of particle identification and tracking is also included. The analysis is performed using the full data set from the initial Xe-Xe research phase that took place at a collision energy of 5.44 TeV. A precise calculation of the relative yields of various particles is provided, accompanied by a comparison of their momentum patterns. A systematic comparison of the relative yields of these particles across different event types is also presented, including the classification of events into different categories of collision intensity.

The behavior of parton distribution functions at low momentum fractions can be understood by utilizing intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Intrinsic characteristics refer to parton properties inherent to the hadron, whereas extrinsic factors arise from kinematic constraints imposed by the momentum transfer in scattering processes. In this study, we provide a theoretical framework that bridges perturbative QCD descriptions to confined parton models, allowing PDFs to evolve based on both Markov process-like interactions and instanton-mediated mechanisms. Our analysis reveals that even in a perturbative QCD context, parton evolution along the Bjorken direction is non-Markovian due to the impact of higher-twist corrections. By incorporating higher-twist terms into the PDF evolution equation, our formalism becomes non-linear and non-Markovian, capable of addressing the emergence of parton interactions and their role in evolution. Intrinsic factors are rooted in parton interactions that can be understood within the context of effective theories, where extrinsic factors, associated with kinematic constraints, are accounted for through the boundary conditions inherent to the evolution equations.

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, in the form of disks, were subjected to different thermal treatments in a vacuum environment to study the effect of temperature on their microstructure and mechanical properties. This was achieved by simulating the solidification process using X-ray computed tomography to analyze their internal structure and test their mechanical properties for strength, hardness, and elasticity. The results showed that increasing the temperature from 800NC to 1200NC resulted in a significant microstructure transformation, with the specimens reaching maximum strength and elasticity at 1100NC and 1200NC respectively, with elastic moduli 5.5 times and 2.6 times greater than the untreated materials. Furthermore, the findings showed that the optimal sintering temperature varied depending on the composition of the simulants with optimal results for the Martian simulant being 100-100NC lower than for the Lunar simulant. This study's outcomes will contribute to the understanding of how simulants are affected by high-temperature processing in vacuum conditions and has important implications for building structures on other planets and in space.

The adhesion between a liquid droplet and a solid object can either slow down or intensify a particular process depending on the surface properties of the objects involved. This project investigates how a liquid layer on a fibre influences droplet breakup, a process that can be exploited to create microdroplets. Our study shows that a static fibre coated with liquid will experience an instability when an additional amount of liquid is added to it. This phenomenon is caused by an interaction between two competing factors, the increase in liquid height and the drop-like shape assumption, that triggers liquid slippage over the fibre. Our analysis accounts for all possible scenarios of liquid slippage using a theoretical model and provides detailed results for a particular type of liquid.
