The Greek mathematician George Polya discovered that any function which is periodic with a complex variable and takes on positive values, can be expressed as a combination of the functions sin and cos, multiplied by exponential functions with complex variables. Researchers later generalised Polya's result to functions which take on any real values, by proving that such a function can be expressed as a combination of Gaussian functions in two complex variables, multiplied by periodic functions with a real variable. We have extended Polya's result to groups of one-dimensional local compacity, by proving the equivalence of two conditions for a function defined on such a group to be expressible as a combination of Gaussian functions in two complex variables, under certain constraints. Our result includes the cases of the circle, the real line, the p-adic line and the p-adic circle.

Presence-absence data is represented as a binary matrix where each row denotes a sampling location, and corresponding columns represent different species or ecological components. The overall structure of the data sets can significantly impact the results of further ecological analysis. Therefore, it is crucial to carry out dimensionality reduction or cluster the data at a sampling level to gain insights into the spatial patterns or gradients of biodiversity. This research aims to find an appropriate clustering method for dimensionality reduction by comparing its performance with other top clustering techniques using stability and predictive measures. The assessment of various clustering methods was performed on high-dimensional data sets with relatively few replicates, and candidate clustering methods were evaluated based on their consistency, clustering quality, and relevance to ecological research. Ultimately, our study validates the utility of these clustering techniques and provides a framework for selecting the most suitable approaches for future presence-absence data sets.

In recent years, salient object detection has been extensively researched, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often hinders the progress of method development and data collection. To overcome this, this paper proposes an efficient unified framework for both tasks by integrating cross-modal information in a self-attention context. This framework leverages a cross-modal attention module to fuse RGB and depth information, resulting in improved image quality and performance. Notably, this framework allows for direct prediction on RGB-D images, sidestepping the need for separate training and processing for RGB and depth images. This flexibility, combined with its simplicity and speed, gives it a significant advantage over existing methods.

The second Affect in DBPaaS Challenge tasked participants with predicting the
aggressiveness of consumer reviews on the basis of labels provided in a
classification task. Our team, UM-IU@LING, submitted entries for both the
subtasks of the challenge. For subtask A, we utilized a BERT-based classifier
pre-trained on a sentiment dataset, while subtask B's results came from an
evaluation of multiple SVM models using different characteristic sets. 
Our submissions achieved 0.884 and 0.897 accuracy in subtasks A and B, 
respectively.

A number, N, can be defined as a palindrome if its decimal representation reads the same from left to right as it does from right to left. This note explores two distinct types of integer quotients resulting from division by a single digit divisor, D. When the divisor, D, is an odd palindrome, the resulting quotient, Q, must itself be a palindrome. Conversely, when D is an even palindrome, the resulting quotient, Q, may take on two forms - either it is a palindrome, or it is not.

Computed Tomography (CT) scans combine data from multiple energy sources and suffer from noise, which hinders accurate readings. To address this, we've developed a unified framework for both single- and multi-source CT systems that reconciles discrepancies between various energy spectra and filters out measurement noise. Our approach involves a system-wide minimization scheme to determine and distinguish between materials based on known and unknown energy profiles. We've tested our method on artificial and genuine data and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in recovering original images, matching expectations, and identifying materials with minimal error.

This work presents a novel approach to handwritten text recognition (HTR) that relies on a single model to simultaneously recognize languages, segment translated phrases, and eliminate duplicates, all without requiring any specific language model pre-training. By incorporating automatic language identification and word-level segmentation guided by lexical statistics, the model's output is refined and filtered. Furthermore, to minimize the need for extensive training, the method leverages existing knowledge of lexicons and grammars typical of European languages. Evaluations on diverse datasets indicate that this approach achieves acceptable accuracy levels, with results comparable to those produced by more complex pipelines for languages like Portuguese and Greek, and superior to those for German.

Using the GW approximation combined with configuration interaction methods, we combine density functional theory and atomic physics approaches to study the electronic structures of heavy nuclei. Our simulation of the isotopic chain of $^{187-209}$Tl considers exchange, spin-orbit interaction, and an effective atomic potential. By adjusting the atomic potential to match experimental data and employing a rigorous methodology for wave function regularisation at the surface, we achieve a high level of accuracy within the GW framework. Our study examines the regularisation's impact on results and outlines the significance of surface effects. The calculated atomic masses are compared to experimental values, yielding an average difference of 0.11 meV, with a 10-fold reduction in uncertainty following the regularisation adjustment.

Concepts in topological quantum phenomena are increasingly explored in quantum electronics due to their potential for fault-tolerant quantum computing and unique electronic properties. The Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model has served as a primary tool for conceptualizing the ideas of topological quantum phenomena, as it is straightforward to solve and exhibits prominent effects of electron-phonon interaction. This review delves into the SSHE model to clarify the underlying assumptions of topological quantum phenomena and related concepts, as well as their practical and theoretical implications. The review covers key aspects of the SSHE model, incorporating contemporary extensions that incorporate electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions to address the following questions: (1) How do various conceptualize topological quantum phenomena, as related to periodical systems? (2) What are the necessary requirements for a conceptualized topological quantum charge? (3) How can these concepts be applied to a solitary periodical system, such as the SSHE model? (4) What are the practical and theoretical implications of the various interpretations of topological quantum phenomena? The discussion is joined by a list of editor-approved publications related to topological quantum phenomena and the SSHE model.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with bounded, convex domains in $\mathbb{C}^n$ and unit disks in $\mathbb{C}$. A composition operator is defined as a mapping that takes a function to a function composed with another function. We determine operator compactness by investigating the behavior of its finite hybrid Toeplitz and Hankel matrices, drawn from symbolic objects, which in this context, are weighted bi-overlapping covering systems of divisors. If a weighted bi-overlapping covering system of divisors has all associated weights greater than a certain value, its associated Hankel matrix is invertible, indicating that the composition operator is compact. Conversely, if a weighted bi-overlapping covering system of divisors has at least one associated weight less than this value, its associated Hankel matrix is singular, implying that the composition operator is not compact. We also establish that the compactness of a composition operator on a Bergman space is equivalent to the compactness of an associated finite Hankel operator on a weighted Bergman-Hankel Hilbert space. This relationship allows us to leverage existing research on Hankel operators to better understand compactness in composition operators.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method employed involves calculating a two-loop amplitude in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory and then using a projection operator to obtain the supergravity amplitude. The approach relies on an accurate calculation of the preamplitude, which includes accounting for boundary terms in the AdS Heun equations. The solution of the Dirichlet boundary problem yields a characterizing function enabling the identification of the amplitude via the Witten solution, ultimately facilitating the extension of the technique to higher-loop amplitudes.

This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed for efficient memory usage on GPUs with multiple threads. Unlike other allocators that rely on global memory allocation, DynaSOAr creates blocks of contiguous memory through local allocation, enhancing performance and reducing errors. The allocator is compatible with C++ and can be used with existing code, including a test suite demonstrating its efficiency and accuracy. DynaSOAr is particularly suited for real-world applications involving multiple threads, as shown in a real-world example with source code included. The implementation and performance of DynaSOAr are discussed in detail, along with results from various benchmarks and the test suite, which showcase its performance advantages. Overall, DynaSOAr offers an efficient and accurate memory allocation solution for GPU programming.

We explore various standard $U(1)_X$ models derived from the $SO(10)$ framework, incorporating gauge symmetries $SO(10)\rightarrow SU(3)_C\otimes SU(2)_L\otimes U(1)_E\otimes U(1)_X$. The choice of $U(1}_X$ embedding is dictated by three distinct conditions: (1) presence of an additional $U(1)$, (2) breakdown of SO(10) to SU(3)_C \otimes U(1)_L included in the maximal subgroup SU(3)_C \otimes SU(2)_L \otimes U(1)_X, or (3) form of the extra $U(1)_X$ linear combination. We examine the possibilities for baryon number assignments to three matter fields in each scenario and determine the resulting number of baryon number dark sectors, while also analyzing the possible electric dipole moments and constraints on the $(g_X/g_L)$ parameter resulting from neutrino masses, vacuum stability, and unitarity bounds. Finally, we investigate the potential exclusion of the models by LHC and future cosmic microwave background observations.

A comprehensive analysis of a pressurized cane, made of isotropic material, is carried out using Eulerian finite element methods. The calculation of longitudinal tension and mechanical stability under increased internal pressure is performed. The investigation focuses on the effects of internal pressure, material properties, and boundary conditions on the stability of the structure. Furthermore, the study offers insight into the feasibility of growing cane plants with imposed bending, which could enhance their structural integrity.

In various fields, ensuring the reliability of decisions made with incomplete knowledge goes beyond standard risk management, prompting researchers to seek more comprehensive safeguards. We suggest a two-pronged approach for mitigating uncertainties in decision-making tools (DMTs). Firstly, we outline a framework for confirming a DMT's robustness, which involves evaluating the consistency of its guarantees with the uncertainty principle. Secondly, we demonstrate that robustness assurances can be provided through the approximation of uncertainty bounds via probabilistic circuits. Our method involves relaxing constraints in relation to circuits, enabling the computation of tighter upper bounds on uncertainty measures such as the Wasserstein distance and maximum conditional mutual information. Our approach, demonstrated through network example, allows DMTs to operate within time and space complexity limitations, thereby providing practical decision-support tools that can effectively handle intricate scenarios.

Waves in a solid medium can be seen as exhibiting Weyl particles, where previously disconnected points in momentum space are connected, resulting in Weyl points forming along the Brillouin zone's boundaries. This occurrence can be replicated using ultrasonic double-momentum-space Weyl points by adjusting momentum and pressure, where a zero-line appears in the acoustic tensor's eigenvalue spectrum. This new development has led to theoretical predictions of acoustic Weyl insulators and an associated Weyl node-based Weyl semimetal-to-insulator transition. Additionally, observations of Weyl nodes have been linked to Weyl point-mediated Weyl node lines and Chern gaps, suggesting that Weyl nodes can appear in thermal spectra and contribute to Weyl node lines forming in momentum space. This concept has been grounded by experimenting with two types of elastic mediums, where Weyl nodes have been observed in both cases and their features matched to predicted Weyl node behaviors.

Researchers classify the automorphism groups of the 22 generalized quadrangles that possess a neighbor-transitive abelian group. Furthermore, the paper describes the codes and partial spreads resulting from these quadrangles, given a specific generating vector. The work also determines the codes and partial spreads resulting from the quadrangles defined by their vertex stabilizers.

Located at the core of our galaxy, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) exhibits a crucial role in understanding stellar evolution and development. This distinctive region within the galaxy's center can be characterized by a distinct density pattern that varies significantly in different directions. This anisotropic density framework is vital for grasping the CMZ's structural features. In a new study, researchers analyzed the Correlation Function of the CMZ's stellar distribution to quantify this anisotropy. Their analysis revealed a connection between this anisotropy and the galaxy's rotational velocity. Additionally, based on the anisotropic density framework, the team created a set of modified radial profiles. These modified profiles can be compared with actual observations of the CMZ to further refine its characteristics. By employing the anisotropic density framework, researchers can make more informed predictions about the CMZ's future evolution.

High-fluence experiments with ultrafast X-ray pulses can lead to excessive absorption, causing distorted XANES signals due to excited electronic states. The intensity of X-ray pulses necessary to produce these distorted spectra, however, is relatively low. This research presents a mathematical model describing the density of electron groups during high-fluence X-ray absorption and utilizes it to create a computational tool for determining electronic probabilities. The tool is then employed to develop a correction method for recovering the genuine XANES signal from experimental data affected by elevated photon flux. The proposed algorithm is straightforward and efficient, with a relatively minimal computational burden. It can be applied to a broad range of systems and is versatile, allowing modification to accommodate distinct physical scenarios. The mathematical model and computational correction method were tested using simulated and genuine XANES data obtained at the Mn L-edge in methylaminoacet acid, a manganese(II) compound.

A microtemperature detector has been developed using a single 0.35$\mu$m standard CMOS process, featuring low power consumption and a minimal area. The design employs a novel two-stage sampling technique to achieve a high resolution and low error tolerance. The temperature sensor incorporates an internal reference voltage generator that produces 1.8V, which can also function with an external reference voltage input. The design has successfully passed temperature accuracy testing under both controlled and varying conditions. The performance results include a 0.6V-1.8V operating range, 0.24{\deg}C resolution, {\pm}1.4{\deg}C average temperature inaccuracy, 1.06nJ per conversion energy consumption, 0.38nA standby current, 2.5ms conversion time, 2.5ms standby time, and 0.03{\deg}C/\sqrt{Hz} noise. The design's area is 0.031mm^2, meeting the requirements for resource-constrained IoT nodes.

Quantum entanglement, a fundamental aspect of quantum physics, holds great promise for the advancement of various cutting-edge technologies. Research has yielded a plethora of entangled states, each carrying unique benefits and drawbacks. Polarization entanglement, specifically, plays a vital role in the development of all-optical quantum computers and metrology systems. The present study seeks to combine the merits of both quantum scissors and NMR-based polarization entanglement, seeking to integrate the versatile functionality of quantum scissors into a platform heralded by a proven entanglement tool. Our research achieves this by substituting quantum scissors, traditionally used for segmenting and manipulating entangled states, with a new entity: the quantum scissor. The new entity enables the conversion, suppression, and detection of polarization entanglement in a single process. The proposed method necessitates the utilization of mixed polarization states, necessitating the adoption of a novel Fock-space-based approach for calculating entanglement quantities. The study concludes with predictions regarding the execution of the protocol using currently accessible infrastructure.

This paper explores digital euclidean spanners, which are similar to traditional euclidean spanners but constructed using binary codes instead. It defines a binary code as suitable if any two encoded points at a distance less than epsilon from each other are also at a distance less than epsilon in the digital space. Building on earlier research, we develop two methods for creating such codes and demonstrate that they result in o(log/epsilon) dimensionality, which is close to the lower bound of omega(log/epsilon) proposed by Bronstein and Roldos. Additionally, we adapt these codes to create constant factor spanners in digital spaces.

Accurate classification in IoT is crucial, but it's hampered by costly computations and excessive feature sets, which need to be trimmed for efficient operations. Selecting essential features reduces both the complexity and expense, enabling efficient processing on resource-constrained IoT devices. However, choosing the optimal feature subset is a time-consuming process, requiring efficient techniques to minimize expenses. This research introduces a new forward feature selection method that efficiently reduces computation and memory usage, making it accurate and reliable. The proposed method compares itself to existing techniques using six real-world datasets, outperforming them in terms of accuracy and misclassification errors while minimizing storage and processing costs.

Godel modal logic builds on Godel algebras, with their non-distributive, de Morgan, and complemented lattice foundation, by incorporating right division as an additional binary operation. Beyond the standard Godel algebra operation set, Godel modal logic allows the utilization of an overbarred form of right division. This paper delves into the characterizations of both normal and non-normal multi-modal Godel algebras through their representation as subsets of direct products of Richard's algebras. It also explores the first-order syntax and semantics linked to these algebras, with a focus on both normal and non-normal logics. Additionally, the paper discusses the topological spaces naturally derived from these algebras in relation to preorders specified by the hypersequence property.

This research presents a system that facilitates word alignment in diverse languages, relying on external bilingual sources. To achieve this, our model generates words from visual contexts and links them to corresponding words in translation, drawing from a vast range of bilingual datasets. We've tested our system in two languages and discovered that it can accomplish word alignment with a single image, and also improve existing translations by leveraging visual information. By integrating external data, our model can manage languages not sufficiently represented in extensive monolingual datasets.

We suggest an imaginative algorithm named the Distorted Resolvent Algorithm (DRA) to solve Nash Equilibria issues. The DRA is constructed around the residual function of a monotone, Lipschitz operator, similar to the Extragradient Algorithm, yet distinguishes itself through distorted steps that accelerate convergence at the expense of precise data recovery. Incorporating a parameter for consistency, the DRA ensures robustness in the presence of data distortions beyond mere inaccuracy. By studying the DRA's properties as a parameter is continuously varied, we gain insight into its long-term behavior. Specifically, when the distortion diminishes to zero, the DRA converges to a Nash Equilibrium, while remaining resilient against limited data distortion. Conversely, when the distortion surpasses a certain threshold, the DRA converges to a equilibrium distorted by the same amount. Our research is grounded in the study of Nash Equilibria in games with Lipschitz potentials, providing a framework for understanding the DRA's performance. Moreover, we illustrate the effectiveness of the DRA through numerical experiments in both single-player and multi-player games.

A subtype of dark matter consisting of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) poses a theoretically constrained scenario, with multiple gravitational wave detectors potentially capable of detecting PBH-based dark matter. The predictions for signal and background event rates, including estimates for false positives and noise, can be generated using the tool referred to as 'Pete', and expanded upon in the code known as 'PopSyCLE'. This code enhances Pete's capabilities by incorporating additional substructures for PBHs and allows for the computation of substructure-dependent signals. Further developments in PopSyCLE consider various types of PBH masses based on different formation mechanisms. This research employs PopSyCLE to examine the predicted signals and background event rates for the case where PBHs constitute all of dark matter, specifically looking at the breakdown of false positives according to type, and comparing the predicted rates to current limits from the LIGO, Virgo, and geo-based gravitational wave detectors. Six different PBH mass functions are examined, each based on distinct formation mechanisms including: 1) equal-mass symmetries in mass distribution, 2) a single mass corresponding to early universe matter-radiation equality, 3) a range of masses tied to early universe matter-radiation equality and set by local over-densities, 4) a range of masses tied to early universe matter-radiation equality and set by cosmological modulated initial conditions, 5) a range of masses tied to early universe matter-radi

In a system where rigid wedges are formed from spheres, with openings that vary in size, we analyze the phase transitions that occur as the wedge angles are adjusted. Despite the complex geometry, featuring irregularly shaped constrictions, simulations reveal that Ising-like phase transitions arise, with two main phases developing - a low-density swarm phase and a high-density hexagonal close-packed phase. Unusual features emerge when the density and sphere diameter are varied: (1) the density of the swarm phase exhibits a minimum as the sphere diameter increases, with behaviors transitioning between two distinct types of swarm phases; (2) a pressure increase causes the swarm phase to transition directly into a hexagonal close-packed phase, bypassing an intermediate Laves phase; (3) at specific wedge angles, a hexagonal close-packed phase coexists with a pair of phases featuring different splay modulations in a stable equilibrium.
Kunsch, O. and Nigro, S. and Simmanner, G. and Waldinger, F.

A persistent challenge in quantum optics remains the development of visualization methods that accurately represent quantum states without compromising their properties. We propose a protocol using a single, light-sensitive pixel coupled to a quantum system that enables visualization of any quantum state without compromising its undetected photons. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through successful measurement of the Wigner functions for both two-photon and single-photon states. Our method relies on a combination of Mach-Zehnder interferometry and photoconductivity, offering a promising quantum-resource platform.

This study investigates the source of increased friction when a liquid foam is pulled through a narrow channel, revealing that the enhanced friction exceeds expectations based on the foam's viscosity. The research decomposes the friction into components caused by liquid bubbles and a foamy layer, revealing that the latter dominates at lower velocities. A model is developed to explain how the foamy layer's texture produces anisotropic stress, leading to increased friction. The model matches experimentally determined friction values accurately.

This study proposes an AI framework for identifying abnormal skin cancer samples using entropy, with the goal of detecting atypical skin cancer images to aid human dermatologists in their diagnosis. To address the issue, we developed a classification framework that assesses cell disorder and uses this information to determine outlier samples. Furthermore, we investigated the performance of integrating this assessment with traditional deep learning classification methods. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of combining cell disorder evaluation with deep learning, revealing substantial improvements in classifying atypical images and pinpointing outlier samples through entropy-based analysis.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier experiments. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models that can predict the behavior of almost-free electrons in the presence of correlations and verify their agreement with experimental data. Additionally, our results confirm that the enhancement of electronic mass due to long-range interactions remains negligible in this specific material.

Microcanonical ensemble calculations are typically restricted to systems with constant energy, also requiring the total number of particles, volume, and number of degrees of freedom to be specified. A therapeutic approach for processing MC simulations has been developed which enables the transformation of trajectories from one ensemble to another while overcoming the challenge of altering the system's phase space volume. Alternatively, an ensemble transformation method has been devised that utilizes a Hamiltonian dynamics approach, allowing for the direct creation of trajectories within the desired ensemble without the need for phase space volume changes. We specifically examine the application of this method in the context of a free-evolving isolated system that undergoes a transition from a confined to an open state, expanding infinitely in the latter scenario. The newly devised approach overcomes the limitations of existing methods, such as the inability to change the system's volume without also altering its microstate, an issue that has previously presented an insurmountable obstacle in the calculation of correlation functions and other MC simulation-based quantities. The potential scope of applications for this method extends well beyond the realm of free-evolving systems, encompassing a wide range of one-dimensional, multi-dimensional, and nanoscale systems.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on weighted contributions. The weights calculated belong to the class of multiple zeta values, as they involve iterated integrals, which are a fundamental concept in this field. The study demonstrates that all non-zero weights can be expressed as a product of two components: a graph-related value and a value associated with a differential form that has been explicitly defined. The paper offers two primary avenues for further research: first, determining the structure of the differential forms, and second, proving a conjecture regarding a specific pattern of graph-related values.

This research explores solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially small oscillations, in two precompressed systems based on a timber model and a diatomic granular chain. These solitary waves occur when two opposing waves with equal amplitudes cancel each other's displacements, resulting in a state bounded by exponentially small oscillations. By applying the nondegenerate match of matched asymptotics, we prove the existence of these solitary waves and provide estimates that validate their behavior through a series of expansions.

A theoretical model, the classical cosmological collider, predicts that primordial scalar fields will be generated at high energies during an inflationary period, resulting from the collision of particles and their antiparticles. The peaks of these scalar modes, represented by discrete quantum numbers, can be observed in the universe's primordial power spectrum and provide insight into the underlying particle physics that existed during the high-energy period. The primordial features in this theory are classical signatures that can be detected in future surveys, such as the PRISM project, and once primordial features are identified, they will reveal the masses of non-relativistic particles that existed in the early universe. The paper investigates possible patterns in these primordial features, their potential interdependence, and the constraints that can be imposed on their masses by the requirement of particle stability. The study also explores the limitations of current understanding and the future prospects for primordial feature research.

Consider a graph G upon which a 2-factor has been imposed, resulting in alternating paths that create "valves" within the graph. For the purpose of our investigation, a graph G is referred to as an accordion graph if it comprises a 2-factor along with a Hamiltonian cycle that intersects the 2-factor at exactly one point, effectively creating "squeezed" regions in between. Our analysis demonstrates that these graphs exhibit the property of being non-self-complementary as well as non-planar, with the possibility of constructing them starting from any given quartic circulant graph that happens to be non-planar and possesses a specified characteristic. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the sought-after accordion graphs correspond to a specific subset of graphs known as naga graphs, characterized by their absence of triangles and quadrilaterals, with an underlying constraint that they are also non-planar. Our method for producing accordion graphs yields an infinite class of accordion graphs, classified as quasi-face-trans graphs that happen to be both star-free and triangle-free. Notably, our work also touches upon the pairing in these graphs, which we refer to as "squeezed pairings," along with proving a specific conjecture regarding the class of accordion graphs known as Acc.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the synthetic wavefront emitted by a point source in three-state quantum walks with periodic boundary conditions. Our investigation reveals that the correlation function behaves similarly to a Gaussian distribution at early stages of the walk. By examining the scaling properties of the correlation function, we identify two distinct regimes: one dominated by a deterministic wavefront and another characterized by a randomly fluctuating front. Our analysis enables us to derive a critical time mark separating these regimes, and further, we leverage finite-time scaling techniques to derive scaling laws for both regimes. Our discussion is accompanied by numerical simulations validating our theoretical findings.

Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures are currently receiving a great deal of interest due to their capacity to tackle large-scale image classification, beat convolutional-based networks, and extract robust image features for downstream tasks. Nevertheless, ViT requires substantial training data labelled as unlabelled, pre-trained on a large dataset such as ImageNet-21K, to acquire inductive biases. When applied to tasks that haven't been seen during training, ViT sometimes struggles to perform well, indicating that more work on understanding its internal processes and developing training methods is needed. This study investigates how ViT extracts features from its training corpus by studying degenerate, semi-simplified variants of ViT, and reveals that the transformer structure of ViT generates meaningful features related to image classification. Moreover, the team behind this study introduces the concept of emerging attributes, i.e., new attributes that appear during the training process, and observes that the variation in learned features in ViT is largely due to attributes already included in its labels, with the variation being largely due to noise. Furthermore, the team introduces the concept of momentum-batch enlargement (MBE), i.e., using labelled images produced by moving and transforming training data to enhance learning, and this method enhances the performance of ViT on unseen tasks by using these artificial images in conjunction with regular data augmentation. Experimental results show that MBE boosts the performance of ViT on the ImageNet-1K challenge by 4.4% and also improves its robustness to

A proposed unified dark matter model is introduced, combining the concepts of dark matter and dark energy. This model, however simplistic, is shown to accurately match the observed cosmological data as well as the gravitational effects described by Newton's and General Relativity theories, from the sub-microscopic planetary scales up to the macroscopic cosmic levels. A numerical analysis reveals that the model's parameters are heavily interdependent, implying any variation in one parameter affects the others. A zero-coincidence parameter regime is identified, characterized by the following features: a lower bound on the unified dark matter mass, a specific range for the interaction timescale, and a corresponding range for the modified force sensitivity. A challenge inherent to the model arises from the need to observe or experimentally verify the unified dark matter, presenting a current void in experimental research but offering future possibilities with advancing technology and astrophysical surveys. With anticipated advancements in technology and astrophysical observations on the horizon, the unified dark matter can potentially be directly investigated, providing essential confirmation or refinement of the model.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when measured in certain types of Sobolev spaces and an associated H^1 space, thus confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

A recent breakthrough came when the Stable Diffusion model demonstrated exceptional image creation abilities and efficiency, compared to previous approaches. Given its potential to transform the digital creative industry, we explored the challenges of developing reliable automated image creation tools. We identified "stylistic event disruption" as a key issue, where the model's style is disrupted due to external factors, resulting in poor results. To address this issue, we developed the "Stable Creator", a groundbreaking system that utilizes reinforcement learning to control the model's semantic direction, thereby disrupting unwanted styles and stabilizing the model's creations. We tested the system's effectiveness across various scenarios, including integrating human feedback, and found that it consistently outperformed baseline creations in producing results that align with intended semantic directions.

Recent advancements in image processing technology, driven by deep learning, have led to cutting-edge techniques like image concealment methods utilizing analytical techniques to restore degraded images after a prediction step. These methods have demonstrated exceptional performance, but traditional non-parametric approaches struggle with reliability due to inconsistent predictions. In contrast, a new strategy based on Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offers a robust solution by generating multiple predictive paths, thereby ensuring reliable forecasted images. In this research, we explore BNNs as a solution for reversible concealment, focusing on deriving a feasible approximation for sampling-based prediction and analyzing its theoretical implications. Experimental outcomes confirm that BNNs produce high-quality concealment results with minimal artifacts, and their samples serve as effective noise sources for diverse concealment methods, such as optimal concealment.

Our research focuses on the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter, led by a new process considered by the Particle Data Group. We analyze this process within the frameworks of effective field theories for neutrinos and dark matter, incorporating observations from J=1 meson decays by the BESIII collaboration. Our study takes into account existing limits imposed by J=0 meson decays as well as searches by the BESIII and LHCb collaborations for invisible J/ψ decays, as well as research using the Sun by the BESIII collaboration. We determined that J/ψ decays into invisible matter offer more stringent constraints on certain types of effective field theories for neutrinos and dark matter than similar analyses based on lepton decays of J/ψ and dark matter searches in the Sun. We discovered that J/ψ decays into purely invisible matter set the most restrictive constraints on Wilson coefficients related to vector and scalar operators among effective field theories for neutrinos and dark matter. Moreover, J/ψ decays into purely invisible matter set the most restrictive limits on coefficients related to curvature and Higgs-dimension operators among effective field theories for neutrinos and dark matter.

Solar magnetic bright points represent localized areas of enhanced brightness due to the non-uniform distribution of magnetic fields in the solar photosphere. Their identification has the potential to provide insights into underlying mechanisms, such as field fragmentation, realignment, and interaction with surrounding plasma. Observations of these features in the solar photosphere have revealed a wide range of brightness values, from slight enhancements to several percent, depending on previous detection methods. In this study, we analyze data from the SOT/Hinode and pynoia projects, presenting a comprehensive two-dimensional histogram of magnetic bright point properties in Figure 1. The resulting distribution appears as two distinct parts: a lower-intensity section with a broad range of sizes and orientations, and a higher-intensity area with a narrower size range and predominantly horizontal orientation. The separation between these sections becomes more pronounced at higher intensity levels. Based on these findings, we propose that the first category comprises magnetic bright points with various sizes and degrees of intensity, while the second category likely consists of shorter, horizontal magnetic bright points resulting from the interaction of stress and shear in the solar atmosphere.

Human visual processing of moving images, particularly when it comes to distinguishing between animate and inanimate objects, has been largely unaffected by advanced deep neural networks, which have achieved impressive results in computational analysis of motion. Researchers investigated whether dynamic visual cues play a crucial role in distinguishing between living things and non-living objects by creating minimal films, short, concise video sequences that convey strong animacy or inanimacy cues. These films were then shown to both humans and machines. The study revealed that humans rely heavily on dynamic cues, whereas machines, powered by deep networks, primarily rely on noise-sensitive context, rather than the intended animacy or inanimacy cues. The findings indicate that current deep learning methods are not yet effectively utilizing motion information, and the study presents a new benchmark, called the minIFlow dataset, consisting of highly compact animacy cues, available at https://github.com/epfl-vl/dynamic-bias.

Dark matter composed of magnetic monopoles, originating from a simple superstring theory, is investigated under the assumption that no large-scale cosmic magnetic fields exist today, except for local, galaxy-scale regions where the magnetic energy is comparable to that of regular dark matter models. We analyze how the magnetic monopoles' non-Abelian charge and the breaking of gauge symmetry influence the dark matter cross-talk with matter, especially through direct detection experiments and the microwave background observations. Ultimately, we determine the possible mass and charge ranges of the magnetic monopoles that could fit recently measured data from such studies, including the monopole's interaction strength with electrons.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the video transformer framework. By exploiting inherent temporal and spatial correlations within weather time-series sequences, we employ the video transformer with cross-attention adaptation to extract predictive patterns. Furthermore, we introduce a weighted hierarchical sampling strategy to refine local low-resolution features and enhance the model's overall predictive capabilities. To address the issue of shift-sensitive receptive fields, we incorporate a modular cross-attention unit with the ability to control spatial and temporal dependencies. Our proposed model outperforms existing benchmarks, demonstrating improved forecasting accuracy for both numerical and categorical weather variables.

In models featuring three Higgs doublets, we discover that the low-energy behavior of dark matter can be attributed to either a composite inertino or a fully inert triplet particle. These particle physics models, extending the $S_3$ symmetric three Higgs doublet model, incorporate one dark matter candidate, which has a charge of $Q = 0$. We analyze the possible dark sectors resulting from these models, which may be verified by upcoming experiments such as the LUXe, XENON1T, and SPICE experiments. We also find that the models providing fully triplet dark matter are compatible with the latest constraints from relic density, direct detection, and indirect mono-$Z$ particle detection at least when non-standard Higgs interactions are negligible. However, the model featuring the composite inertino may satisfy these experimental requirements, provided that certain parameters are within specific ranges.

A fundamental hypothesis known as the PPT quadrilateral conjecture holds that any quadrilateral formed from entanglement operators using PPT regions will have all its vertices occupy PPT territory. It's proven correct for specific examples involving Ising and free fermion models.

In neurons, the process of substance transport is crucial for maintaining homeostasis, but disruptions caused by traffic jams or blockages can lead to imbalance and contribute to neurodegenerative diseases. Understanding the regulations exerted by neurons on transport mechanisms is essential, but current models simplify this control for the sake of computational feasibility. By employing a novel formulation, we develop a comprehensive optimization model that incorporates this control function and facilitates quantitative analysis between the efficacy of different regulations. Furthermore, our model reflects the real-world scenario by incorporating bounds and uncertainties, which are addressed through a two-stage approach. By testing our model against comprehensive simulation cases, we validate its accuracy and demonstrated its utility for investigating the effects of different regulations on substance transport. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the quantitative evaluation of substance transport regulations and their impact on neural function.

Significant topological features in complex network structures, such as clusters and patterns, have been widely recognized by researchers, but their actual implications in networked systems remain understudied. Our investigation focuses on analyzing network motifs – recurring, tiny patterns within networks – and their potential to answer inquiries in intricate network contexts. We devised a test scenario set in a financial market network and found that network motifs showed the ability to respond to requests for information, with the most efficient patterns being those featuring a limited number of interconnected elements. It has become evident that incorporating motif-based decision-making into decision-making processes can be beneficial, especially in situations involving limited information availability. We believe our results will inspire future researchers to delve into the world of intricate network dynamics and uncover the secrets hidden within complex, topologically linked systems.

In a binary system consisting of a white dwarf and a black hole, we examine the process of a white dwarf losing mass due to tidal forces as it orbits the black hole, causing emission of gravitational waves. This process results in the white dwarf losing mass, leading to a reduction in its mass. Concurrently, the black hole gains mass through the absorbed matter, which affects its rotation rate and further influences the white dwarf's evolution. To better understand this process, we developed a numerical model and implemented it in a computer code that simulates the binary system's behavior. Using this code, we modeled a specific white dwarf and black hole binary system and tracked its development over a considerable period of 54 billion years, observing the white dwarf's mass decrease and the black hole's increasing mass. Our model also accounted for the emitted gravitational waves and showed that the radiation it produces follows established emission patterns.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, can provide insight into these processes. Studies of weak electromagnetic interactions rely on form factors to describe the hadronic part of the final states, which can be further understood by decomposing the hadronic current into specific orbital angular momentum components. Given the increasing data availability from future experiments, a new description of the hadronic currents is presented in terms of the quantum numbers of the final hadronic state using the isobar model. Additionally, the work includes formulas for orbital angular momenta and the rules for describing the decay chains of arbitrary mass hadronic three-body systems, which also improves existing descriptions in terms of form factors.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the Shorley metric, a measure of text similarity, by combining the Jaccard distance and the normalized Camille Adrien distance. We generalize their research by developing a family of parametrized Tversky metrics, incorporating the Jaccard distance as a special case. Additionally, we demonstrate that one member of this family corresponds to the normalized information distance used by Cover and Thomas (1975).

Modern image de-blur techniques fall short in dealing with real-world, high-quality blurred images of dynamic scenes. These methods either rely on time-of-flight or depth sensors that aren't typically used in smartphone cameras, or assume access to high-frequency image data, making them ineffective for real-world applications. To overcome these limitations, we developed a novel approach to remove blur using a motion estimator and a pseudo-blur synthesizer, without requiring additional 3D information. The motion estimator employs a neural network to classify each pixel's motion state and estimate the blur radius, while the synthesizer generates blurred pixels based on a limited set of predefined kernels. By combining these components, we created a data-driven image de-blur algorithm and evaluated its effectiveness on a dataset of 400 synthetic images and a separate set of 200 real-world images, outperforming existing methods in both synthetic and real-world tests. The code and dataset are publicly available at the link provided.

This study showcases an advanced molecular circuit capable of replicating the complex behavior of a learning spiking neuron from the Leaky Integrate-And-Wire model. The sophisticated molecular system, constructed with bistable membrane properties and dynamic synapses, mimics a biological neuron's functionality, including membrane potential modulation, synaptic plasticity, and temporal spiking responses. Furthermore, this circuit's capabilities are expanded to enable self-organizing map algorithms, allowing for the exploration of pattern classification and clustering behaviors.

Let's consider two fundamental ordered sets, $X$ and $Y$, and their respective ultrapowers $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ based on a non-principal ultrafilter. This paper explores how the structure of $\mathcal{X}$ compares to $\mathcal{Y}$ in terms of chain segments, and provides essential examples and counterexamples to support key findings. One notable outcome shows that even with a minimal ultrafilter, the ultrapower of $\mathbb{Q}$ under its standard ordering can exhibit any desired density level in its completed version.

The growing datasets, differences in hardware, and variations in programming languages all contribute to the complexity of evaluating benchmark performance.
As a result, selecting the most suitable benchmark profiling method for a specific use case becomes increasingly crucial.
Traditional approaches, such as comparing various profiling techniques, may overlook the inherent characteristics of datasets, potentially leading to inaccurate conclusions.
Given the significance of data-driven applications, it is essential to develop a systematic method for identifying the most effective profiling strategy tailored to a particular dataset.
This study provides an in-depth analysis of the factors influencing profiling and proposes a comprehensive evaluation framework to determine the most suitable profiling strategy for a specific dataset.
Ultimately, the research identifies particular profiling methods to be the most effective for a range of benchmarking functions, including memory-related, parallelism-related, and prediction accuracy-related scenarios.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been strengthened by a series of inequalities suggesting that if a graph has t colors, it must contain a complete graph with t-k colors for any positive integer k. Researchers previously demonstrated that if a graph has 4 colors, it must contain a complete graph with 2 colors, and now it has been shown that if a graph has 5 colors, it must contain a complete graph with 3 colors.

This research introduces an advanced generalized correntropy-based algorithm for graph signal reconstruction that is adaptable, robust, and efficiently learns the kernel width. In our proposed method, the width of the kernel is initially set as $\sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{n}}$ where $\sigma^2$ is the variance and $n$ is the number of nodes, for signals following a Gaussian distribution. The kernel width was then optimized using the kernel alignment technique, resulting in a value of $\sqrt{\frac{1}{2\ln(n+1)}}$. However, this value may lead to overfitting and oversmoothing, hindering the reconstruction performance. Our study, however, develops a learning approach for the kernel width, $ \sigma^2$, by maximizing the correlation between the original and reconstructed signals, subject to the signal's statistical properties, thereby effectively improving the kernel width. The optimized kernel width enables our algorithm to achieve superior reconstruction performance, benchmarked against existing state-of-the-art algorithms.

A major limitation of traditional interferometry based on spin is the inability to accurately measure entangled states due to detection noise. We've developed a new technique using a entangled spinor interferometer that overcomes this problem by generating customized quantum states. By accurately producing entangled quantum states, we're able to enhance the precision of phase measurements, even in the presence of noise. We've accurately created key quantum states, such as the singlet and Noll-Hofmann state, despite 85% of expected clicks being irrelevant data. We've also successfully made measurements on both the phase and spin components of an entangled quantum state, demonstrating the full functionality of entangled spinor interferometry.

The purpose of this research paper is to derive sharp estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first eigenvalue problem with a nonlinear Robin boundary condition. This involves making precise and rigorous the approximate ideas discussed in a previous paper (Pancol, 2021), using new estimates for the first Dirichlet eigenvalue and convergence results for eigenfunctions.

Deep Neural Networks have surpassed human performance in many areas, but their workings remain difficult to grasp. In an effort to make them more understandable, researchers have focused on interpreting the inner workings of Neural Networks, specifically by analyzing the effects of individual layers. This has led to significant advancements in uncovering network motivations, constraining neural models, and improving quantum algorithm designs. This study examines Graph Convolutional Neural Networks, a type of model that expertly analyzes complex graph-based data. Despite its effectiveness, the concept of GCNNs is complex and difficult to comprehend visually. We present a simplified approach to GCNNs by drawing a parallel with the Matched Filtering method used in signal processing. This analogy facilitates the derivation of Matched Filtering Neural Networks, which match conventional GCNNs in many cases. By breaking down GCNNs into its core components, researchers can better understand this powerful tool and make further advancements.

Unexpectedly, the accuracy of dependency parsing tasks on low-resource languages has been consistently boosted by models like Universal Dependencies. This success can be attributed to pre-trained models, which provide representation capabilities, and the adaptive dependency parsing algorithm, which effectively guides dependency parsing without annotated data. However, the models require a sizable parallel corpus between the target language and a similar high-resource language to achieve acceptable results. In this research, we combine deep contextualized self-learning with dependency parsing to overcome the limitation of limited cross-lingual data. The method employs self-learning to generate pseudo dependencies from sentences with no annotations, which are then refined by relying on the representations of sentences with annotations. This approach enables models to learn dependency parsing purely from raw text, which in some cases includes no annotations at all. Experiments on languages with very limited cross-sentence parallel data show that the method is capable of producing accurate pseudo dependencies, which ultimately results in acceptable parsing performance.

Using the Diquark Model, we've investigated the transition form factors of $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ and found the results to be in agreement with available data. The calculation involves light-front quark model interactions without corrections, such as those involving soft photon interactions. The study includes a Diquark interaction component with a confining kernel, and we've considered several forms for the quark distribution function within the $B\to D$ transition. Notably, we've discovered that form factors obtained using a quark distribution function with a nonzero slope $\alpha'$ differ significantly from those obtained without this parameter. Specifically, we've observed that the ratio $f_+(w)'/f_+(w)$ is zero order $\alpha'$ but becomes negative and increases in magnitude with higher $\alpha'$ order. This shift has significant effects on processes like $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ and has implications for measurements of $B\to D$ form factors. Additionally, we've used our results to make predictions on the behavior of $B\to D$ semileptonic form factors at tipically large recoil energies.

We're investigating a quantum field theory where the gauge symmetry isn't preserved under time evolution, resulting in two distinct forms of BRST symmetry. By utilizing a brane construction, we present a method for identifying novel solutions to BRST cohomologies that translate to physical states with memory, describing charged particles moving through time. Our work draws from elements in ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, u(2) Chern-Simons theory, and the Wess-Zumino gauge.

Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) is considered the most promising extension of Monadic Second Order Logic (MSO) for its potential to describe decidable fragments of MSO. A key feature of CPT is its ability to reference dynamic variables in a choice of equations, enabling the manipulation of partial functions and relations. Researchers have made significant progress in CPT by developing a solid foundation, yet its core question remains largely unanswered: Can CPT decide any non-empty MSO class? 

Our work addresses this question by demonstrating that CPT can express the parity of an oriented graph, a problem traditionally associated with fixed-point logic combined with counting (FCP). To achieve this, we introduce a new fragment of CPT, called Cumulative CPT (CPTc), which includes recursive references to the cumulative computation process. 

We then prove that CPTc is equivalent to a fragment of Choice Less Polynomial Time with Magazines (CPT-MGM), which was shown to be within polynomial-time relative to the size of its input graph. As a consequence, CPT-MGM can be expressed in a new, weakly symmetric fragment of symmetric circuit logic, which in turn implies its lower-time-complexity bound of $\tilde{O}(2^{n^(omega)})$.

In this study, we investigated the property shift from an insulating state to a metallic state in EgBxPyIr2O7 (EgBcPy = 0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) using hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy (HAXPES) and revealed that the final stage of the insulator-to-metal transition occurs at BcP = 0.25. Our HAXPES analysis required 300 eV photons and showed that the samples were measured when insulating state characteristics vanished. Our HAXPES results confirmed that the insulating state transitions to a strong correlation metallic state at BcP = 0.25. We observed a significant increase in the near-core spectral weight (NW) within this metal state, which indicates a substantial enhancement of the low-energy weight in the metal state $\sigma$-band. Our in-depth HAXPES data revealed that the metal state exists over the BcP range 0.25 to 0.75 and that the NW in the metal state starts to decrease at BcP = 0.75. We used this information to develop a phase diagram for EgBcPy Ir2O7 and identified that the metal state exists at BcP = 0.25 to 0.75 with a potential Weyl semimetal state at BcP = 0.5.

Theorems on the existence of Lipschitz selections for low dimensional set-valued mappings over certain classes of core-compact spaces are established. These results are reinforced by an example. To prove these theorems, a new concept is introduced, denoted as $(\rho,{\mathcal A},{\mathcal F})$-core-compactness, which serves as a topological characterization for the core-compactness of the space ${\mathcal M}$.
