The Cyclic Poisson distribution is defined as $f(x;y) = \frac{\exp(-\theta y + \theta x^2}{\sqrt{2\pi}x}$ for $x \neq 0$, with its likelihood ratio being constant, not dependent on $x$, which makes it nonparametric in one dimension, although it still employs parameter $\theta$. The nonparametric case of the Cyclic Poisson distribution has weaker assumptions than others with similar properties, such as the von Mises and Cauchy distributions, which have distinct parameters governing concentration and tail behavior.

Software systems utilizing runtime configuration files can benefit from compile-time customization, eliminating the need for manual tweaking. Our research investigates whether compile-time tools can automate runtime settings, without necessitating expert knowledge. We introduce CLTS, a compile-time system capable of specializing runtime setup files. The CLTS system is composed of two components: a profiling runtime and a generative compiler. The profiling runtime generates a detailed report of runtime parameter utilization, which serves as input for the generative compiler. Our CLTS implementation is applied to three prominent open-source projects, demonstrating its capability of automating runtime setup customization. Our study indicates that a substantial portion of runtime configuration files can be fully automated, while some settings require user input due to complexities involving context-specific information and dynamic changes.

Light dark matter particles are likely to interact with nuclei only weakly, but may freely interact with electrons. This property could be leveraged in sensitive electronic direct detection experiments that focus on searching for dark matter interacting directly with electrons within a nucleus. By doing so, researchers may be able to directly detect dark matter particles in the sub-GeV mass range. This method has the potential to be competitive with other direct detection methods that involve only nuclear scattering, especially in the case of lighter dark matter masses. Furthermore, it is not subject to the same constraints as direct detection experiments that involve only nuclear scattering, such as those related to astrophysical particle velocity and supernova constraints, opening up possibilities for improved sensitivity. In fact, even in the most constrained scenarios, the potential sensitivity of these electron direct detection experiments could surpass that of other direct detection experiments by at least an order of magnitude. Therefore, it is crucial to conduct further analysis to determine the theoretical limits of sensitivity for these electron direct detection experiments. This involves exploring the theoretical limits of sensitivity for various models of dark matter-electron interactions, as well as evaluating the relevance of existing and planned experiments. Specifically, we have examined the potential sensitivity of the CRESST, CDMS Heat, and SYMPHONY experiments, all of which focus on detecting dark matter interacting directly with electrons within a nucleus. In doing so, we have developed new theoretical limits of sensitivity for dark matter masses ranging from approximately two-thirds of the nucleon mass up to approximately one

This paper proposes a method to produce maximum entanglement in the two-qubit XC-X/Y model, which is also known as the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, by adjusting the phase of the driving field in the cavity. It is found that in this configuration, Rabi oscillations similar to the ones observed in the Jaynes-Cummings model occur, but with the entanglement and transmission properties reversed. Furthermore, the findings suggest that in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, there is no net transmission of photons, whereas in the Jaynes-Cummings model, there is a net transmission.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases, making it critically important for monitoring cardiovascular health. Existing research has demonstrated that deep learning methods outperform traditional machine learning in analyzing time-series data. A novel deep learning approach is introduced in this paper for estimating inter-beat intervals from ECG signals, leveraging a "Tiramisu" model previously unexplored in the context of PPG/ECG signals. By utilizing ECG signal data from the MIT-BIH dataset and PPG signals from the HARP public database, this study confirms the efficacy of this model in achieving high accuracy and superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, the proposed model exhibits reduced error rates of $3.04e^{-3}$ and $1.12e^{-2}$ for inter-beat intervals and standard deviations, respectively, thereby showcasing its practical value for clinical heart rate monitoring. Furthermore, the findings highlight that deep learning models can facilitate straightforward and efficient training.

We examine the difference in work done by a active particle on an external force in two cases: one where the active particle's motion is corrected to be overdamped and another where its motion is correctly described as stiff damping. We find that the discrepancy in work done by an external force in these two scenarios can be attributed to introducing a thermal noise with varying intensity. Interestingly, our findings also reveal that the average power input by an external force to the active particle in the correct scenario aligns with the average power input in the overdamped scenario, indicating a form of work conservation.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset containing over 2000 diverse video sequences capturing human body movements from five distinct viewpoints. Comprising multiple categories with varying levels of complexity, HUMBI includes five subcategories: simple, medium-level, and three instances of more intricate movements. To ensure data reliability, each video sequence has been carefully annotated with three independent label applications. Our primary objective is to tackle the problem of 3D human gesture recognition in the real world. This dataset and related challenge provide researchers with invaluable tools to improve existing deep learning-based 3D human gesture recognition pipelines, thereby advancing the field. Recognizing that, although achieving high accuracy may be achievable in controlled environments, it may not be attainable in real-world scenarios where the task requires concurrent movement recognition and viewpoint prediction. To this end, we propose a novel challenge centered on generating robust gesture recognition systems capable of adapting to various viewpoints. This includes classifying gestures across different viewpoints and generalization performance across viewpoints. Our benchmark challenge is centered on achieving this real-world scenario, where we evaluate models based on their accuracy regardless of the camera viewpoint, utilizing HUMBI for model training and testing.

Many researchers agree that incorporating prior knowledge is essential for achieving significant cross-lingual transfer in NLP, but the type of knowledge and how it's presented has varying levels of usefulness. A recent study demonstrates the benefits of using task representations, previously absent from the discussion, as a form of guided transfer. We build upon this study by exploring the potential of task representations as weak guidance for model-agnostic cross-lingual transfer. Our results show that incorporating task representations consistently enhances the model's performance across four NLP tasks and five target languages, with gains often exceeding 5% in NLP metrics such as F1 score and accuracy. We also discover that the effectiveness of task representations is resilient to various forms of perturbation. To facilitate future research, we also present a unified dataset for NLP tasks across multiple languages, known as NTrix, consisting of 11,000 instances.

A key video super-resolution technique, VSR, has been widely recognized for its ability to restore high-resolution images from low-resolution video inputs, leveraging temporal information to generate sharper results. VSR techniques have demonstrated significant performance gains with the integration of advanced network architectures and temporal propagation methods. Our proposal, BasicVSR++, builds upon the BasicVSR model, initially presented in 2020, by refining its propagation and alignment components to produce superior VSR outcomes. In tests using the top-ranked evaluation tool, NTIRE, our model achieved outstanding performance, claiming the top spot in the VSR category for RGB images and ranking second only to a more complex model, VQSR, in the VSR (TCN) category.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using separate models for each task can lead to a phenomenon known as catastrophic interference, where previous learning interferes with new tasks. Our research reveals that this interference is primarily caused by the storage of action-value functions in each model. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel approach where a central module stores a shared high-level policy and the tasks only learn the task-specific differences in their local reward functions. This modular design enables the development of robust multi-task reinforcement learning algorithms that can learn models based on reward shaping and integrate them into a unified framework. Our theoretical analysis confirms that the modular structure substantially reduces catastrophic interference. Experiment outcomes also demonstrate the benefits of this modular design, allowing it to solve more complex multi-task reinforcement learning problems compared to standard methods.

We have improved the performance of finite-time thermal engines by limiting the speed of heat transfer and work exchange. A new method for optimizing the heat and work generated during a finite time period involves restricting the controller, a crucial component that dictates how much heat is released or absorbed and how much work is generated. By addressing the optimizer, we have developed a general approach for optimizing the performance of thermal engines. Our analysis encompasses the most common types of heat transfer and reveals that optimal results can be achieved with minimal effort when the controller is not bound. Additionally, we have investigated the practical implications of optimizing the controller and discussed the key characteristics necessary for optimal results.

This research proposes a spatial analysis for investigating the combined impact of hurricanes and storm surges on power systems. To simulate real-life scenarios, the study generates large-scale datasets of hurricane-related storm surges, utilizing empirical modes method and statistical analysis to determine actual surge heights based on historical weather patterns. These results are further combined with actual wind data from hurricanes to evaluate system performance. To facilitate spatial analysis, the study creates maps of hurricane conditions, including storm surges, and integrates these into power flow calculations via a proposed formula. To verify the accuracy of these findings, the study conducts thorough simulations, focusing on specific areas such as New York and Florida to determine performance metrics and identify key factors, which can inform utility planning and inform strategies for assessing and mitigating potential disruptions caused by hurricanes and storm surges.

This article explores a variation of the Three Balls Conjecture within the context of Clifford analysis. Specifically, we examine a function's behavior in a specific order, given its compliance with specific symmetry and antiderivative constraints in a specific geometric configuration.

We investigate two modifications of the heterochaos baker map, one where the domain is partitioned into two regions of unequal size, and another where the scaling factor differs from the transverse direction. We show that in the former case, the system's ergodic maximally entropy invariant measure can be expressed in terms of the parabolic and elliptical subfields produced by the map's graph, and this measure is expressed in terms of continued fractions. We derive the condition under which this measure is accessible, and find that this condition is met for all sufficiently large entropy values. However, as the entropy approaches its maximum, there exists a critical value beyond which this condition is not met, and this critical value is approached through an asymptotic analysis involving the distribution of parabolic and elliptical subfields. We compare this analysis to a similar problem on the Dyck system, and extend the result of Armandello, Bonacini, and Guarino that the system's ergodic maximally entropy invariant measure is unique to a family of measures defined on the system's 'tree' structure.

Several areas where an expanded scalar sector might exist will be discussed, 
along with prospects for discovering such sectors at future high-energy colliders. 
The possibilities include expanded sectors from local $U(1)$ symmetries, 
dark matter coupled to an expanded sector, and interpretations of dark matter observations 
that involve an expanded sector. Potential signs of an expanded sector, 
such as its contribution to $2\ell+2\nu$ events in higgs-boson decays and 
two-gauge-boson decays with extra jets or photons, will be discussed, along with 
predictions for searching for an expanded sector at future colliders through 
associated production of a standard model higgs boson and for direct production.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent filtered convolutional layers. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolutional layers with autoregressive probabilistic modeling. However, the model's pitch control is restrictive due to its hierarchical structure. We propose WPNet as a solution to overcome this constraint. WPNet includes pitch-dependent, expanded convolutional layers that can model circadian rhythms, allowing for pitch control at multiple scales. We also introduce RQNN, a refinement network with a dynamic RQ structure, to model residual signals at various pitch levels. RQNN's R structure represents the common residual signal across different pitch levels, while the Q structure represents the pitch-specific residual signal. We incorporate RQNN into WPNet to enable quasi-periodic signal generation. We evaluated our model using the WSJ0 and LJSpeech-1 datasets and compared it to WN and hierarchical WN with pitch control. The results show that WPNet outperforms the baseline models in terms of signal quality, freedom, and naturalness.

Recommender systems face a critical issue where users' diverse preferences often lead to suboptimal movie selections due to a lack of comprehensive knowledge about each user's preferences. Biclustering has been proposed as a method to address these challenges by identifying co-clusters of users and items that exhibit synchronized behaviors. However, traditional biclustering approaches overlook the variability in preference across users, resulting in an incomplete understanding of each viewer's true preferences. This study presents a novel framework that leverages user-specific biclustering based on the combination of intrinsic and extrinsic characteristics of users, alongside data from multiple sources. By integrating this approach with rating prediction, the proposed recommender system achieves improved accuracy and performance on real-world datasets.

The CORALOPES project is currently conducting a comprehensive study of Earth-like planetary habitability, focusing on the effects of magnetic activity on available light and its impact on detecting exoplanets. Using CORALOPES data, we analyzed how solar activity influenced the spectral distribution of solar features, and explored its impact on detecting exoplanets or characterizing planetary atmospheres. This was achieved by simulating the spectral features of solar faculae and spots using 1D models and a realistic atmospheric model, and incorporating these into the noise model for future ground-based spectroscopic missions. Several new activity indicators were identified that could be observed through spectroscopy, including the [Fe I] 5434.52 and [Fe I] 5555.31 lines, which we recommend incorporating into the analysis of future ground-based spectroscopic missions. Additionally, we observed that the facular and spot distributions identified in the CORALOPES solar data were not uniformly distributed across the solar disk. This was confirmed by the observed correlations and variations in activity indicators, and may be attributed to the rotation and movement of active regions across the solar surface. This could have significant implications for modeling solar activity and may be relevant to other active stars.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves exchanging the normal electrodes in tunneling spectroscopy with highly resistive electrodes during the measurement process. The high resistance in the transport path under these resistive electrodes arises from quantum dissipation due to the exchange of momentum with the surrounding heat bath. The scenario of a Majorana island subjected to this resistive tunneling shows significant differences in its spectral characteristics from the scenario without resistive tunneling. Specifically, for resistive tunneling, the desired zero-energy peak associated with Majorana may be replaced by an non-zero temperature peak with a tunable position and height that depends on the resistive tunneling strength, whereas without resistive tunneling, the zero-energy peak associated with Majorana may be obscured by high non-zero temperature peaks. Our approach thus aims to improve the ability to identify Majorana by introducing distinct signatures that can be easily observed in tunneling spectroscopy.

Marking a functor adds structure to it by establishing a universal path, and this concept extends to bicategories through the use of shadows, which can be seen as bicategorical marks. This paper delves into the properties of shadows, demonstrating that they behave similarly to classical marks and have equivalent applications, such as marking subcategories and functors. In addition, the paper connects shadows to virtual and exotic marks, offering a new perspective on these concepts from the bicategorical mark perspective.

A significant trend in image editing is style transfer, aimed at merging two images into a single output. While forward style transfer takes two images as input, inverse style transfer utilizes a single image with a specified style. Due to their diverse applications, it's challenging to address both problems with a single model. To bridge this gap, we propose learning a neural network that can extract a style from a pair of images, making it applicable to both forward and inverse style transfer with a single, compact model. Our model can produce notable results for both tasks, as demonstrated in the experimental section, where the quality of the generated images is higher than that of existing models. Additionally, our code and model will be publicly available.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task in the LOVEU challenge, which was evaluated at the 2022 IEEE Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. The report outlines the proposed model's architecture and details its implementation, also highlighting the key challenges encountered during the competition. The target goal of this competition was to synthesize robust word-level speech magic models for spoken word recognition, with the particular challenge being to develop models that could effectively handle out-of-distribution data.

This research focuses on the process of snowfall, where particles are dropping through atmospheric turbulence. Previous studies had mixed outcomes when applying the concept of selective sweeping, a phenomenon where different particle sizes respond uniquely to flow patterns, to explain settling patterns. A detailed, time-resolved analysis was conducted around a targeted snowfall event, capturing both particles and flow data. Measurements revealed evidence of selective sweeping, with larger particles reacting primarily to downward flow patterns and smaller particles also being influenced by sideways flows. A theoretical model, however, struggled to fully reproduce the observed data.

In situations of limited knowledge or restricted time, robots must make early decisions about ongoing activities to ensure they reach their destination in time.
We have developed a novel approach, called DAP, which integrates planning and learning to forecast a target trajectory for the robot. DAP consists of two key components: 
A deep detection network identifies critical obstacles within the robot's path and pinpoints its location.
A prediction function, powered by reinforcement learning, adjusts the trajectory based on the obstacle's actual state instead of the robot's initial estimate.
By processing real-time sensor data, the robot constantly refines its navigation course, resulting in improved timing and lowered collision risk.
We tested DAP on a simulated environment and achieved the most accurate predictions among compared methods.
Additionally, DAP demonstrated superior timing and collision avoidance capabilities in various scenarios.

In triple-plane sparse tomography (TPC), scanners with limited memory can lead to processing overload due to the arrival of three sparse images simultaneously. A solution to this problem is found in Bicephalous Convolutional Autoencoder (BCAE), an innovative deep learning framework. It consists of an auto-encoding mechanism where data is broken down into features, compressed, and then reconstructed from those features. By optimizing the reconstruction process, the algorithm fine-tunes the spatial resolution and intensity of the compressed images. Consequently, the model can extract meaningful patterns from the scan data and efficiently eliminate irrelevant details. This results in significantly reduced data without compromising image quality or resolution, allowing for clearer and more distinct features in the resulting images. Our experiments with synthetic and real-world data have shown that BCAE outperforms traditional data reduction methods.

Building on previous work, the Finzi gravity model has been further developed by incorporating the effects of galactic clusters on dark matter distribution. This theoretical framework aims to reconcile the varying radial profiles observed in galactic clusters. This work employs the Finzi gravity model to analyze the dark matter distribution of galactic clusters using the Navarro-Frenk-White and Einasto models. To verify the model's predictions, a statistical test was conducted to compare the resulting radial profiles with observed data on 13 galactic clusters. The outcome indicates that neither the Navarro-Frenk-White nor Einasto models can accurately reproduce the radial profiles of all galactic clusters, as evident from the statistical errors obtained. Nonetheless, the analysis shows that the real-space slopes of the Einasto model match the predictions of the Finzi gravity model more accurately than those of the NFW model.

A type of geometric hypergraph is one where the intersections of its components resemble geometric shapes. This encompasses a range of applications, from the study of interconnected components in images to the investigation of certain types of networks. This paper explores a particular class of geometric hypergraphs linked to a problem originating from Tardos and Shor's study of a game. We identify challenges in fully resolving the problem and propose a related issue concerning the maximum number of 3-element subsets with a specific property within a set of n integers. We refer to this as the k-GEQ3 problem. Our proposals for addressing this issue include a upper bound based on a general approach for such problems and improved but still limited estimates derived from examining the specific structure of the k-GEQ3 problem.

To investigate particle-income patterns, the densities of low-lying states in $^{61,62,63}$V nuclei were calculated using the South Florida quantum shell-model. These studies reveal that unpaired  $p$-orbit protons in the $^{51}$V parent nucleus contribute to the angular momentum transfer, resulting in the excitation of a $d_{3/2}$ proton relative to a $d_{3/2}$ neutron. As a result, angular momentum-aligned $^{6}$Li targets can yield either head-on or tail-on couplings with significant $\alpha$-particle production. Analysis suggests that the $\alpha$-production cross-section is optimized at an energy near the Coulomb barrier, with the cross-section influenced by the specific relative atomic mass of the $^{6}$Li and $^{51}$V nuclei. These findings demonstrate that Li-V systems can serve as relevant models for studying particle-income patterns and can provide insight into the $\alpha$-process in heavy elements.

Inspired by the self-looping behavior of Pacific Lamprey, this study develops a robotic system with a unique combination of a flexible rod and adjustable cam follower. The research investigates the conditions that drive the lamprey's comparative advantage in climbing on curved surfaces through analytical assessments, simulations, and practical tests. By integrating this innovative mechanism into a robotic platform, the study demonstrates the feasibility of this device in navigating curved surfaces through visual guidance.

A new methodology, centered on a stochastic Fokker-Planck equation, is proposed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in colon cancer by analyzing their impact on the dynamics of the tumor's growth and the patient's immune response. 

Colon cancer, one of the most prevalent form of cancer in adults over 50 years old, is driven by a flawed adenomatous polyposis coli gene regulation system that creates polyps which can develop into a tumor, leading to severe immunological reactions, necessitating treatment to mitigate the patients' suffering and ultimately their mortality rate. 

To model this process, a research team uses a stochastic partial differential equation, known as the stochastic Fokker-Planck equation, to simulate the behavior of colon cancer cells and the patients' immune response under various treatment conditions, based on historical data, and develops a simulation tool to visualize these scenarios. 

By optimizing the variable parameters in the model, the researchers find the most effective treatment combinations that minimize the patients' mortality and discomfort, based on the patients' medical history and treatment outcomes. 

An open-source version of the simulation tool, known as ColCan, has been developed and made available for scientific research purposes, enabling scientists to experiment with different models and explore new treatment options. 

The proposed ColCan tool is centered on collaborative research between physicians, patients, and data scientists, with a focus on identifying data-driven personalized treatment combinations that can be verified in clinical trials and ultimately used to develop personalized treatments for

Optimizing Wireless-to-Wireless transmission strategies is crucial, yet their efficient exploitation is hindered by limited understanding of Age of Information (AoI). To address this, we develop a hybrid approach combining symbolic and numerical methods within the framework of Berge's Conflict Graph. Symbolically, we identify the age optimization as an integer programming problem with fixed costs and flows, subject to constraints. Numerically, we employ Deep Learning techniques to solve this problem, given the computational infeasibility of finding an optimal solution. By training a neural network on historical problem solutions, we enable it to efficiently solve the AoI optimization problem. Our results show the trained network can resolve the optimization within 10-20 milliseconds, allowing us to incorporate it in a D2D optimization algorithm with minimal computational overhead. Our simulations reveal the success of this hybrid approach, as the trained network allows us to reach an efficient trade-off between timeslots allocated to D2D and Wireless-to-Wireless transmissions, not achievable with conventional symbolic or numerical solutions alone.

This research proves that helicity is preserved in the compressible Euler equations for smooth solutions with any spatial and temporal regularity. Moreover, it demonstrates the local $C^\infty$ well-posedness of the helical smoothing operator, a tool employed to establish conservation of helicity. The development of sophisticated frequency splitting and frequency localization techniques plays a key role in this proof.

For the Davey-Stewartson II equations, we find that the reflection coefficient has an absolute value of more than one in specific situations, which happens when certain conditions are met regarding wind direction and depth. The background three-dimensional flow meets certain criteria, and as a result, so does the two-dimensional perturbation. The circumstances in which this occurs involve an infinite number of interactions between waves and the mean flow. The conditions required can be realized through various methods, including altering wind patterns and water depth. The resulting behavior of the reflection coefficient is dependent on the signs of certain key components. The presence of multiple modes in the perturbation affects how the reflection coefficient behaves for different modes. The occurrence of a large reflection coefficient is tied to the presence of perturbation modes that interact in a particular way with the mean flow. The characteristics of these modes determine whether a large reflection coefficient will be observed, and if so, what its value will be. The background mean flow's properties are crucial in determining which perturbation modes will be active and thus influence the reflection coefficient's behavior. The properties of the background mean flow also determine the properties of the perturbation modes, and thus play a key role in determining the reflection coefficient's significant behavior.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems at the threshold of gravitational wave detection reveal that residual eccentricity at the point of detection provides crucial insight into the binary's pre-inspiral history. By utilizing advanced post-Newtonian models, researchers can accurately estimate this eccentricity, thereby enhancing existing estimates based on leading-order approximations. A comparison between these methods shows that accurate predictions for binary neutron star inspirals involving 10 solar mass objects can be achieved with a high degree of precision, specifically better than 10^-5 for eccentricities below 10^-2 and better than 10^-4 for eccentricities up to 10^-2. Furthermore, models that account for higher-order effects in binary masses yield more precise outcomes, particularly for binary neutron star inspirals with masses near equality.

A proposed innovative concept, referred to as the "FEL/OSEMELOY" scheme, involves combining a free-electron laser oscillator with a self-amplification by exponential absorption-based linear accelerator to generate highly intense, fully coherent X-ray pulses. The feasibility of producing extremely short, high-intensity X-ray pulses in this configuration is being investigated. The idea is to have the free-electron laser oscillator feed a gas-based undulator to amplify X-ray intensity, potentially reaching terawatt levels. The feasibility of generating 10-femtosecond X-ray pulses with a 10-gigawatt intensity is predicted using three-dimensional simulations, making way for groundbreaking applications such as nonlinear spectroscopy and absorption spectroscopy.

Detecting unusual incidents in real-time is crucial for effective graph-based network surveillance. Current methods, however, struggle with accurately identifying anomalies on dynamic graphs, which represent changing networks over time. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel approach using a temporal residual graph to represent time-evolving network transformations. Building on this framework, we have developed an innovative anomaly detection method that leverages deep learning with temporal convolutional networks, enabling superior performance that outmatches existing approaches as evidenced by our comprehensive empirical comparison.

This research explores the dynamics of an imploding shock wave in a medium with gradually changing density and finds that finite-size clusters can move towards the center of the implosion. When the average density of the medium decreases as a result of the implosion, large-scale structures emerge from the clusters. The size of these large-scale structures depends on the initial conditions of the clusters and the characteristics of the imploding shock wave. It has been discovered that the formation of these structures occurs through a process similar to the formation of vortices in a jet, involving a balance between the forward force of the cluster and the force exerted by the shock wave. Furthermore, it was found that the shape of the cluster's self-similar profile depends on the index of the fluid's velocity distribution function, whereas its asymptotic behavior is determined by the cluster's size relative to the wavelength of oscillations. It was also found that these results can be applied broadly to a wide range of physical processes involving shock waves.

The growing presence of Artificial Intelligence systems has led to a significant issue, namely their lack of transparency. Users are increasingly demanding that AI systems be able to provide detailed explanations for their actions, which has sparked research into Explainable AI. The growing complexity of AI systems made possible by advances in machine learning has created a significant challenge, as these systems can learn from large datasets and adapt quickly. However, the methods currently used to improve the explainability of AI systems are primarily technologically focused, which neglects the needs and preferences of the end-users. 

This paper proposes a collaborative approach that integrates requirements engineering to facilitate a user-centric methodology for specifying explainability requirements. By drawing on established best practices in requirements engineering, this approach can help stakeholders identify, align, and prioritize the needs and preferences of end-users in relation to explainability. Furthermore, this methodology provides a framework for representing the requirements related to explainability within a unified structure. 

To demonstrate the feasibility of this methodology, the paper describes a practical case study involving collaborative workshops where stakeholders worked together to identify, align, and prioritize the requirements for the explainability of a collaborative robot system. 

The study's results show that this user-centric methodology can facilitate the specification of relevant and prioritized requirements for the explainability of AI systems in a natural and intuitive manner. 

The research contributes to the knowledge in this area by offering a methodology that can assist in addressing the current limitations of requirements engineering in the context of AI systems' explainability.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to tailor clinical treatment and follow-up for individual patients. 
The process of classifying polyps as benign, malignant, or intermediate depends on the evaluation of specific abnormal tissue features in the colorectum.
Developing an automated system for identifying these features in colorectal polyps among other lesions is essential for enhancing macroscopic identification skills.
However, training such a system poses a significant challenge due to the need for annotated data, particularly features relevant to identifying abnormal areas in colorectal polyps.
Consequently, we created UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset consisting of high-resolution digital images of histopathological specimens containing marked areas relevant to identifying abnormal features in colorectal polyps. 
This dataset comprises images of normal, benign, and malignant lesions, along with annotated areas highlighting specific features relevant to identifying abnormal areas and lesions. 
Furthermore, the dataset includes graded annotations detailing the relative distribution of abnormal features in lesions. 
To establish a baseline for our dataset, we conducted comprehensive experiments involving classification and segmentation tasks. 
We found that integrating the gradients for normalizing images significantly improved classification accuracy. 
For segmentation tasks, employing a multi-scale convolutional neural network resulted in higher DICE coefficients. 
We are now inviting researchers to participate in training their models on this dataset.

A covert communication system enables secure information transmission from a sensitive source to a receiver, with the covertext encoder and revealtext encoder designed to appear random and unaware of the secret information.  In our investigation of the optimal covert source coding problem with a jammer, we analyzed data leakage as a graph theory problem and derived new performance limits for existing schemes and proposed the jammed covariance preconditioning method to achieve these limits.  This novel approach differs from previous methods that focused on reducing revealtext activity or covertext entropy.  To illustrate its effectiveness, we conducted numerical experiments on jammed Gaussian sources.

Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images are susceptible to various disturbances during the imaging process. Conventional restoration techniques have been ineffective in producing high-quality results due to the imaging mechanism's inherent complexities. Current automatic image processing methods fall short in their performance compared to human-adjusted outputs. This study presents MrSARP, a cutting-edge deep generative model that prioritizes image realism while facilitating image enhancement. Developed with a bi-layered architecture in mind, MrSARP is designed to mimic the SAR imaging process in a downward manner. Leveraging data-driven training, MrSARP is trained on large datasets containing synthetic data, with its bottom layer generating synthetic data similar to real-world SAR images and its top layer adjusting existing SAR images. To achieve faster convergence and improve image quality, MrSARP incorporates a self-supervised data term into its optimization process. Our experiments demonstrate that MrSARP outperforms existing methods in various SAR image restoration tasks, such as despeckling, dust removal, and focusing correction.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant incorporates quantum systems with classical optimization techniques. By adjusting various parameters, QAOA's performance can be optimized but challenging Bayesian modeling is needed to accurately calculate probability distributions, probability weights, and energy values for comprehensive evaluations. A proposed Bayesian approach assesses the uncertainty of these quantities and offers a reliable framework for quantifying results. This method is applied to a specific problem and compared with the standard QAOA in simulations.

This research develops a method for determining the overlap area between two elliptical shapes, encompassing circular cases as a natural extension. The proposed method calculates the intersection region between two ellipses using a straightforward mathematical approach, facilitating its implementation in computer programs. Additionally, the paper confirms that the central challenge in determining ellipse intersections remains solvable only if one adopts an analytical method similar to the one presented here. The area calculation method derives from analyzing the boundary between the two ellipses as a polynomial of degree 4, then applying algebraic topology to determine the overlapping area, specifically by computing the numerator and denominator of the area expression as polynomials of the ellipse parameters, and finally employing these expressions to calculate the area, which may not always be rational. The method is versatile and can easily determine whether the ellipses intersect, as well as identify all relevant parameters, including tangent points and areas of overlap. The method is demonstrated with actual code provided.

Continuous-duration reinforcement learning presents a persistent challenge due to the inherent ambiguity in time variables. Duration can be conceptualized as a signal similar to image or text data, where a suitable representation is crucial for processing. In our research, we address this issue by applying the q-learning framework to model policies for continuous-duration tasks. Since standard q-learning relies on the use of numerical action spaces, we extend this approach by representing the action space as a signal space, where actions are expressed as time-varying functions. Moreover, we induce structure in this space by modeling actions as piecewise-linear trajectories. Our theoretical findings confirm that a well-designed representation is essential for efficient learning and that a linearly structured action space facilitates this process. Moreover, our research shows that a policy based on this representation can be learned through off-policy training with eligibility traces. We validate these conclusions through simulations involving robotic manipulation in 3D environments.

Quantum magnets' dynamical structure factor is a critical measurement, but making predictions for multi-dimensional models like Hubbard is complicated due to computational and theoretical constraints. This study uses a Monte Carlo method on a 3D triangular Hubbard model with up to 128 spins, considering 9 possible momentum directions for excitations and 57 different energy ranges. The results suggest that the system transitions from a antiferromagnetic long-range order at low concentrations to short-range order with increased frustration at higher concentrations, with intermediate phases that depend on concentration. These findings align with experimental results on triangular lattice materials, such as TbInO3 and GdTiO3, and also with earlier theoretical predictions, including an interpretation that explains how certain patterns emerge through "order-by-disorder" mechanisms.

Vertebral location and identification are crucial for spinal research, clinical practice, and medical imaging technology development. However, identifying these points can be quite challenging due to the intricate structure of the spine. Previous studies often employed model-based or learning-based approaches, but many of these methods are only applicable in specific scenarios, and some rely on excessive computational resources. In an effort to overcome these limitations, this study proposes an advanced vertebral location and identification system, featuring a novel spine alignment process and an anatomically constrained optimization technique. By using adjustable parameters and vertebral center coordinates, the location of all vertebrae can be estimated. To determine the optimal values for these parameters, the researchers developed a specialized cost function, taking into account desirable characteristics such as compactness, separation, and spinal alignment. By integrating this function with advanced optimization tools, the best-fitting parameters can be quickly and accurately identified. Through extensive testing on a large dataset, the researchers confirmed the effectiveness of their approach and demonstrated its superior performance by achieving high levels of accuracy and efficiency. The proposed system showed LIDs accuracy of 97.91% and 97.85% for LID+ and PID+, and 97.87% for PID+ with LID as a by-product, outperforming the benchmark by a significant margin. The study's findings provide valuable insights for developing efficient and accurate spine-related algorithms.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The current generated by these jumps measures entropy expulsion from a system to its surroundings. The paper examines the unconditional averaging of this entropy expulsion, focusing on its dependence on the system's driving forces. The calculation of this averaged current is shown to be independent of the statistical method used, whether it's based on path integrals or state populations. The reason for this independence lies in the current's gauge invariance. Furthermore, the paper proves that extreme-value statistics of the current follow a Gaussian distribution under certain conditions. The proof relies on the stationarity of the underlying Markov process and extreme-value statistics of the jump heights, which themselves are known to follow a Weibull distribution. The first part of the paper lays the groundwork for a companion study, which will use these results to investigate the convergence of limiting statistics in stochastic thermodynamics.

This article extends relative quantum geometry to any birational manifold pair (X, Y) by defining Y-relative quantum fields on X and showing they have a well-structured representation theory. The calculations are worked out in detail for Y-X rational and torsional equivalences. The concept is further generalized to relative cohomology with de Rham realization. The methods employed involve formal calculus techniques and structure theory of Y-X relative ODEs.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can create an undamped acoustic connection that allows for efficient sound transmission between them. This occurs through electrical connections formed across insulating barriers by the materials. Our team has developed models for piezoelectric systems that explain how the materials' mechanical properties interact with produce robust sound transmission. We investigated various configurations of the materials, studying both parallel and perpendicular alignments, and discovered unique phenomena triggered by specific alignments of the materials. Notably, in a particular configuration, the materials can exhibit complete transmission of acoustic waves at a specific frequency.

This article discusses the concept of reservoir photonics, where a system of interacting light and matter is used to process optical information. To explore this idea, we have created a theoretical framework for a specific reservoir photonics circuit, consisting of a gain region and a loss tunnel that connects to an output waveguide. The reservoir is modeled by a BEC of exciton-polariton condensates, formed within a microcavity containing resonant semiconductor quantum wells. The output waveguide then allows for the observation of propagating wave packets, which can originate from either the forward or backward direction depending on the system's initial and resonant conditions. Furthermore, we have examined the emergence of localized wave packets, or "photonic bullets," which can travel long distances with minimal loss in the waveguide, such as in fiber optics. Our analysis of these propagating wave packets, obtained through numerical and analytical solutions, can provide insights into reservoir photonics and offer a promising perspective on light processing and manipulation.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22 b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and loss rate is essential in deciphering the environment that fostered the formation of this debris cloud. In this study, the authors revisit grain growth in the context of thermal structure and dust properties, employing thermodynamic models to predict grain size and number density within the atmosphere of K2-22 b. By incorporating sedimentation and phasing, the authors refine this model and compare it with observations of polarimetry and thermometry during transit. This model predicts a range of large grains ($\sim$ 0.1 - 1 micron), consistent with observations of dust polarization, and suggests extremely high dust loss rates ($\sim$ 1 - 20 metric tons/sec), exceeding previous estimates by an order of magnitude. Maintaining larger grains until later stages is possible if smaller grains are efficiently removed. While several factors may influence the model's outcome, its success in explaining multiple transit observations cannot be coincidental, indicating that its key predictions may serve as a baseline for future comparisons.

We establish a novel criterion, referred to as coherence, for the Milnor fibration in a holomorphic function $f$ from a $d$-dimensional complex domain to the complex plane, specifically under the condition that the critical subspace of $f$ possesses a particular kind of smoothness. This criterion holds not just for polynomial functions, but also for functions that can be broken down into polynomials, often referred to as finitely presented. Notably, this new standard allows us to prove the coherence of $f$, provided it does not have a certain type of singular behavior, known as non-normal singular behavior, throughout a $d$-dimensional space. When applied to a monic polynomial, this coherence implies that the Milnor fibration can be viewed as a smooth, oriented, and stable variation of the zero set of $f$, which has a particular structure. This result enlarges a previously established theorem for multivariate polynomials, specifically those that are quasihomogeneous.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analysis. It enables users to easily work with data using the popular Pandas API they're familiar with in Python. Daany is completely.NET core-compliant, making it highly versatile and easily integratable into various.NET-based applications, including Visual Studio, MATLAB, and Python via the pydaany package. Developed under the Apache 2.0 license, Daany is freely accessible from the GitHub repository <https://github.com/brauny72/Daany>.

I challenge the conventional wisdom that Galileo was a proponent of mathematising physics, arguing instead that he sought to integrate math and physics in a more integrated way. By exploring the broader mathematical context of Galileo's time, I demonstrate that his approach to physics was not uniquely driven by a desire to use math, as was common among his contemporaries. Instead, Galileo's contributions were shaped by a more nuanced understanding of math and physics that was informed by his engagement with the wider mathematical community.

The birth of stars and galaxies is attributed to various complex processes that occurred in the Primordial Universe. For a deeper understanding, researchers have developed mathematical models to analyze these phenomena. To this effect, a new theoretical framework is introduced, based on the Bertrand-Roux distribution, to study the breakdown of thermal equilibrium during the Big Bang. Utilizing this distribution, a precise mathematical formula is derived for the average number of particles in terms of temperature and chemical potential. Building upon the Bertrand-Roux distribution, a model is developed to quantify the occurrence of particle associations, given as a function of temperature and chemical potential. Through this model, the rate of ionization in the Universe is quantified and compared with the standard Saha's model for different temperature variations. Interestingly, both the Bertrand-Roux and Saha's models produce comparable results at high temperature levels but diverge significantly at lower temperatures, indicating the onset of non-Gaussian influences during the Big Bang. These non-Gaussian effects are further exemplified by developing a mathematical model for the standard deviation of the number of particles. The validity of this approach is also verified through simulations utilizing randomly generated data.

This study explores the interaction of two magnetic islands in a collisionless plasma, focusing on how their collision generates complex plasma and magnetic field configurations. Island coherence emerges when plasma frequencies and Alfv\'en speed are comparable, while turbulence develops when there's a significant disparity between these parameters. Comprehensive analysis reveals how an island's internal structure is shaped by various forces, including magnetic pressure, thermal pressure, and electrostatic forces, which are visible in suitably chosen biplots. This study also validates the accuracy of a magnetohydrodynamic model by comparing its results with those from a full MHD simulation, showing that it effectively captures key collision dynamics.

This research introduces Amanuensis, an innovative cooperative system that generates
code while explaining it in detail to the human developer. Its primary feature is
its ability to adapt to the developer's skills, providing clear and detailed
explanations to one another. During coding, the developer enters questions or
doubts about the current code, and Amanuensis responds with a useful reformulation
of the code to address those concerns. Through this process, the system refines its
model of the developer's expertise, ultimately enabling self-improvement. To
demonstrate its capabilities, the researchers evaluated Amanuensis on a range of
programming tasks, including designing a user interface and generating code to
predict user ratings.
